methods.name: Artifact Analysis
methods.imageAlt: Shelf of collected household objects, including figurines, a kokeshi doll, teapots, cups, and small ornaments.
methods.imageSource: Martin and Hanington (2012), Universal Methods of Design
methods.whatItIs: Artifact Analysis is the systematic examination of the material, aesthetic, and interactive qualities of objects to understand their contexts. Essentially, it is utilizing some sort of artifact in order to gain information regarding its substance.
whenToUse: When you are doing anthropological work or using artifacts to inform history.
When you need to examine and compare precedent and competitive products.
When you want to study specific aspects of artifacts, such as materials and manufacturing processes, colors, brands, or online presence.
howToDoIt: Identify the desired result: Decide what question you are asking and what you need to take into account. Write a worksheet in advance to guide the researcher, keep the work on topic, and document only information relevant to the subject.
Analyze the materials: Take a quantitative inventory of the artifacts. Look for defining characteristics, such as material composition, wear and tear, durability, and disposability.

Analyze the aesthetics: Make a subjective visual assessment, and note whether the artifact can be identified with a particular time period or location. Consider how individuals interact with or use the object and what significance it may hold for them.

Analyze the interaction: Examine how the artifact may have been used, how it functions or operates, whether it had a social, shared, or collaborative purpose, and whether there is evidence of misuse, adapted use, or potential adjustments. Ask what the artifact could have been used for and what the human interaction with it was like.

Review your documentation: From the information you collected, decide what the physical, social, and cultural context may have been. Ask whether you need more information and what your analyses revealed.
whatYouNeed: Something to perform visual documentation with (camera, sketchbook, phone, camcorder, etc.)
Something to take notes with (pens, pencil, notepad, journal, etc.)
Artifacts themselves as well as the individual who performs the analysis
tips: Do your best to avoid bias.
Be open to different worldly perspectives, these artifacts may not be something culturally relevant to you and that's okay.
Keep in mind that the artifacts paint a bigger overall picture (Who may have used them and why?).
mistakes: Lacking visual documentation and general notes.
Believing that an artifact cannot be a digital object.
Addressing every aspect of the interrelated qualities regardless of the analysis question.
methods.example: A man discovers that the colonial-era house he converted into a museum has a sealed-off basement full of objects and artifacts. To understand their physical, social, and cultural contexts, he commissions an artifact analysis. After extensive note taking, handling the artifacts, and inspecting their aesthetics and materials, the analysts determine that everything is likely original to the house and that the room was more than likely a sewing room for the maid or the wife of the home.
sources: Djajadiningrat, J. P., Gaver, W. W., & Frens, J. W. (2000). Interaction relabelling and extreme characters: Methods for exploring aesthetic interactions. Proceedings of the Conference on Designing Interactive Systems (DIS '00). https://doi.org/10.1145/347642.347664
Hanington, B., & Martin, B. (2012). Universal methods of design. Rockport Publishers.
Ness, V. S. (2012, December 2). Visual anthropology: Photography as a research method. Academia.edu. https://www.academia.edu/2232044/Visual_anthropology_Photography_as_a_research_method

methods.name: Automated Remote Research
methods.whatItIs: Software collects interaction data from users in their own environments, without a researcher present. Analytics, clickstream logs, and session recordings reveal what large numbers of people actually do, rather than what they report doing. Use it to find patterns worth investigating through follow-up interviews.
methods.reference: Martin, B., & Hanington, B. (2012). Universal methods of design. Rockport Publishers. Method 5, p. 16.
sources: Martin, B., & Hanington, B. (2012). Universal methods of design. Rockport Publishers. Method 5, p. 16.

methods.name: Behavioral Mapping
methods.imageAlt: Floor plan of a grocery store with tracked movement paths, beside photographs of three participants' baskets and counts of items.
methods.imageSource: Martin and Hanington (2012), Universal Methods of Design
methods.whatItIs: Behavioral mapping is the observational documentation of how an individual moves and interacts in the context of their environment. This method produces insights focused on both individuals and the places they move through; it reveals traffic patterns and motivations behind their actions when interacting with a space.
whenToUse: When you need to understand how people typically interact with the physical world to better understand their needs and wants.
When you are working in urban planning, merchandising layout, or service centers.

In the early stages of designing a physical space, a designer can use behavioral mapping on existing spaces that are similar to what they aim to create, and use their findings to begin designing their floor plans.
howToDoIt: Become familiar with the space: Analyze the physical layout of the space and the goals it attempts to achieve through its mapping.
Consult experts: Learn about the main purpose of the space and techniques already put into place to serve this purpose.
Develop a framework: Set a research goal and a methodology on how to discover this when the on-site research is conducted to ensure the results are as effective as possible.
Observe the space: Record the space through video or on-the-ground notes and, depending on the research goal, pay attention to how the space affects the user's physical or emotional behavior.
Analyze the data: Reflect on what the observation stage produced and document it in graphs and maps. Discuss the findings in open-ended conversation with stakeholders and users.
whatYouNeed: Consent to observe a space and the individuals interacting with it
Cameras/video recorders to capture the scene (if allowed)
Notebooks and laptops to make observations or sketches
1-2 on-site researchers to make documentation of the observation
Physical or digital tool to create a floor plan map of the space to display the data found
Transportation to the space being observed
tips: Go into the observation with well-established parameters of what you will be observing, because the goals and nuances of individual actions can become muddy if you are simply broadly observing people.
In individual-centered mapping, to better understand the user, a designer can pair this method with interviews to better understand a user's motivations.
Recording the space is ideal due to the ability to replay the scene when reflecting on the data gathered.
The online software, ePlanning, is a recommended tool to digitally map the data found.
mistakes: Creating an unfocused behavioral map can lead to unclear and unactionable results.
Making quick assumptions about people's actions can often happen; to avoid this, designers should work in diverse teams when analysing the data.
If there are not enough observational tools, like video time-lapse, the researcher could unintentionally fill gaps in the users' behaviors that were not properly recorded.
methods.example: A scenario where this method could be used is if a designer were creating a new layout for a grocery store. They could go about this by setting the goal of increasing sales for the store and then behavioral mapping existing grocery stores in the area to see which products are most popular. Then, with that data, designers can undergo the process of spatially mapping the new store with strategic product placement that is supported by the findings of behavioral mapping.
sources: Martin, B., & Hanington, B. (2012). Universal Methods of Design: 100 Ways To Research Complex Problems, develop innovative ideas, and Design Effective Solutions. Choice Reviews Online, 49(10). https://doi.org/10.5860/choice.49-5403

Shilon, M., & Eizenberg, E. (2024). Advancing Behavioral Mapping a Step Forward: Meeting Urban Planning's Objectives. International Journal of Qualitative Methods, 23. https://doi.org/10.1177/16094069241298054

methods.name: Buzz Reports
methods.imageAlt: Circular diagram of the Buzz Report cycle: explore news and media, collect findings in a report, share with a team, and discuss.
methods.whatItIs: Buzz reports collect what people are currently saying about a topic across formal and informal sources, such as news, social media, and reviews. The method keeps a team informed about changes that happen on a regular basis.
whenToUse: When you need to keep up with current trends.
When you have information and opinions of both formal and informal sources.
When you need to keep organization and structure for keeping your team in the know with the same knowledge.
howToDoIt: Schedule time: Set aside time to go through a variety of sources and media to find the current "buzz."
Review sources: Go through each source to find the buzz. It can relate directly or indirectly to your project, as long as it shows how the world is reacting.
Share information: Record what you learned in documents so the whole team has the same knowledge.
Tag keywords: Tag each team member's notes with specific keywords so they are easy to scan and understand.
Discuss: Meet as a team to talk about what the buzz means and how it could influence your final project.
whatYouNeed: Computers/Phones to find current news from websites and reviews
Current newspapers for current ongoing events that may be helpful
Interviewees to get personal opinions on what is happening in the world
Scheduled time for research and meetings
tips: Cast a wide net, because inspiration can come from anywhere.
Keep an open mind when browsing different sources.
Give each document a specific headline and synopsis so readers can grasp the gist quickly.
mistakes: Not having all team members look for current information around the same time, which can make findings inconsistent.
Searching only for information closely related to your project, which hides the full picture.
Relying on one area for information about the buzz, which can bias your findings.
methods.example: You and a team want to research the importance of going to college and how students handle it. You look at what people online are saying about their classes, any news you see related to information and events about college, and everything in-between.
sources: Kumar, V. (2013). 101 design methods: A structured approach for driving innovation in your organization. Wiley.
Verrocchio Institute. (n.d.). Buzz Report - Innovation Wiki by Verrocchio Institute. Innovation Wiki. https://www.innovation.wiki/en/method/buzz-report/
Zaragozá, R., & Gasca, J. (2014). Designpedia. LID EDITORIAL.

methods.name: Case Studies
methods.whatItIs: A case study is a research strategy that investigates a single event or instance in depth, in its context, using multiple sources of evidence. The case can be an individual, organization, community, event, or process (Martin & Hanington, 2012).
whenToUse: When you are doing exploratory research to understand an existing phenomenon, for comparison, information, or inspiration.
When you are studying the effects of change, new programs, or innovations.
When you want detailed, intensive knowledge about a single instance or a set of related instances.
When you are exploring the social, cultural, and behavioral patterns of specific communities or groups.
howToDoIt: Define the research question.
Select a relevant case, or a small set of cases, for the situation or area of concern. Extraordinary cases and outliers are welcome.
Collect data from multiple, triangulated sources, such as interviews, observations, trace measures, and document analysis.
Study the case in its social and physical context, and organize the data into themes or patterns.
Interpret the findings in relation to the research question, and cross-verify accounts that come from a single source.
Present the case study with supporting evidence, told as a clear and compelling narrative.
whatYouNeed: Relevant data of chosen study area
tips: Use multiple data sources to strengthen credibility.
Keep detailed notes and documentation throughout the process so you do not get lost in the research.
Make sure your findings connect back to the research question.
Design the telling of the case. A well-composed case study reads as a human narrative with vivid details.
mistakes: Using a single case study to fully support or reject a hypothesis.
Relying on only one data source.
Choosing a case that is not relevant to the research question.
Failing to document data clearly.
methods.example: A design team is tasked with designing a new community park in a city. In order to research what does and doesn't work, they conduct a case study of the most popular park in the city. They observe activities and behaviors, conduct user interviews, and provide feedback forms. Their findings reveal a lack of shaded space for gatherings, which leads to a large pavilion being added to the new park.
sources: Simian, R. (2025). Distilling design methodologies for additive manufacturing from case studies. FormAkademisk, 18(1), 23. https://doi.org/10.7577/formakademisk.5681

Baxter, P., & Jack, S. (2008). Qualitative case study methodology: Study design and implementation for novice researchers. The Qualitative Report, 13(4), 544-559. https://nsuworks.nova.edu/tqr/vol13/iss4/2

methods.name: Competitive Testing
methods.whatItIs: Researchers run structured usability tasks on competitor products to establish a performance baseline. Comparing task completion, error rates, and learnability shows where an existing product stands and which conventions users already expect.
methods.reference: Martin, B., & Hanington, B. (2012). Universal methods of design. Rockport Publishers. Method 15, p. 36.
sources: Martin, B., & Hanington, B. (2012). Universal methods of design. Rockport Publishers. Method 15, p. 36.

methods.name: Content Inventory & Audit
methods.whatItIs: An inventory catalogs every piece of content in a system; the audit then evaluates each item for accuracy, relevance, and redundancy. Together they produce a defensible argument for what to keep, revise, consolidate, or retire before any redesign begins.
methods.reference: Martin, B., & Hanington, B. (2012). Universal methods of design. Rockport Publishers. Method 18, p. 42.
sources: Martin, B., & Hanington, B. (2012). Universal methods of design. Rockport Publishers. Method 18, p. 42.

methods.name: Contextual Inquiry
methods.whatItIs: Observation and interviewing combine in the participant's own environment, with the researcher positioned as apprentice and the participant as master. The method surfaces the invisible structure of work: the workarounds, interruptions, and physical constraints that never appear in a survey response.
methods.reference: Martin, B., & Hanington, B. (2012). Universal methods of design. Rockport Publishers. Method 20, p. 46.
sources: Martin, B., & Hanington, B. (2012). Universal methods of design. Rockport Publishers. Method 20, p. 46.

methods.name: Critical Incident Technique
methods.whatItIs: Participants recount specific events that went notably well or notably badly. Anchoring recall to a concrete incident rather than a general impression produces detailed, verifiable accounts of what actually happened and why it mattered.
methods.reference: Martin, B., & Hanington, B. (2012). Universal methods of design. Rockport Publishers. Method 22, p. 50.
sources: Martin, B., & Hanington, B. (2012). Universal methods of design. Rockport Publishers. Method 22, p. 50.

methods.name: Crowdsourcing
methods.whatItIs: Crowdsourcing gathers information from a large group of people, usually through voluntary tasks or data drawn from media, polls, and apps. A large, undefined crowd responds to an open call and completes small tasks, often for a micropayment or non-monetary rewards such as reputation points (Martin & Hanington, 2012).
whenToUse: When you want to learn your customers' insights, because crowdsourcing reaches a large audience.
When you are short on time and need efficient answers to specific questions.
When you want fresh, innovative ideas early on, which also helps highlight issues that may arise later.
howToDoIt: Address the problem or define what you are looking to accomplish.
Gather participants, such as customers, volunteers, and other employees willing to test your ideas.
Conduct your test, noting all opportunities and new ideas.
Critique the new information and refine it into something more applicable.
Share and discuss the results to gather group insights and move production along.
whatYouNeed: Possible documentation or data collection (note-taking, an app, a platform, recordings)
tips: Communicate clearly with participants. The process should be straightforward for them to understand.
Be open-minded, because success is not immediately guaranteed. You will learn new things and may need to adjust your process.
Set a realistic plan to begin with, to give yourself guidelines and standards.
Offer an incentive or reward to boost cooperation.
Keep tasks uncomplicated, because simple tasks attract the most volunteers.
Include questions with a verifiable answer so you can flag nonsense responses from volunteers who rush.
mistakes: Being vague or communicating poorly with participants, which breeds confusion and complicates the process.
Setting unrealistic standards for yourself, such as for time or materials, which creates complexities you may not be ready to handle.
Starting without a clear starting point, which creates confusion and wastes time.
methods.example: The mayor of your town assigns you a project in which you have to redesign your local park that's been neglected for years by all age groups. After doing the appropriate research, you decide to use crowdsourcing to gain relative information. You gather your participants at random through an online platform, being sure to include all age groups, and ask for their vote, opinions, and ideas on the park. This outreach to a large group of people successfully provides you with many insights and new information to work with in renovating the local park.

methods.name: Cultural Probes
methods.imageAlt: Pile of returned cultural probe materials, including postcards, maps, and photographs, spread across a table under the caption Figure 6, Some of the returned items.
methods.imageSource: a Google Images search for Bill Gaver cultural probes in action; the original publisher was not identified
methods.whatItIs: Cultural probes are a qualitative research tool in which participants complete creative tasks, such as journaling, mapping, and photography, and in doing so reveal information about their experiences.
whenToUse: When you are in the early steps of a research project and need to explore new problems.
When the topic or information is unclear or unfamiliar to the team.
When you want to learn about participants' thoughts and emotions as they go about daily life.
When you want to find the emotions people feel during a test or the roadblocks they meet during work.
When you want to learn what causes stress for college students, and when and why.
howToDoIt: Define the research goal: Identify what you need to understand or learn.
Design the probe materials.
Assemble kits from those materials for the participants.
Give participants instructions on how and when to complete each task.
Collect all materials when the participants finish.
Analyze the responses and look for common themes.
Turn the findings into design opportunities and options.
tips: Make the kits interactive and eye-catching. Kits that grab attention give participants something to try and learn from.
Avoid assigning too many tasks, which can overload and stress participants.
mistakes: Writing prompts that are hard to follow. When prompts are not simple, participants give less clear and accurate feedback.
Failing to synthesize insights correctly.
methods.example: A design team studies the mental challenges a college student faces while finishing a 50-question English test. Probe kits with journals and cards are handed out so students can write down their emotions and moods. The insights lead the team to develop questions that are more straightforward and easy to understand.
sources: Gaver, B., Dunne, T., & Pacenti, E. (1999). Cultural probes. Interactions, 6(1), 21-29.
Sanders, E. B.-N., & Stappers, P. J. (2013). Convivial toolbox: Generative research for the front end of design. BIS Publishers.
Hanington, B., & Martin, B. (2019). Universal methods of design, expanded and revised. Rockport Publishers.

methods.name: Design Ethnography
methods.whatItIs: Adapted from anthropology, design ethnography involves sustained time spent in a community or setting to understand culture, meaning, and practice from the inside. It trades speed for depth and is suited to problems where surface behavior is easy to observe but hard to interpret.
methods.reference: Martin, B., & Hanington, B. (2012). Universal methods of design. Rockport Publishers. Method 27, p. 60.
sources: Martin, B., & Hanington, B. (2012). Universal methods of design. Rockport Publishers. Method 27, p. 60.

methods.name: Diary Studies
methods.imageAlt: Student writes a dated entry in a spiral notebook on a wooden table.
methods.whatItIs: A diary study is a research method where participants record their interactions and experiences over a set time period. It produces insights into user habits, activities, behaviors, and contexts as they naturally occur over time.
whenToUse: When you need to understand long-term user behaviors or habits.
When studying experiences that occur over time, such as integration in daily routines or product lifetime.
When studying behavior across different contexts, such as time of day, locations, and situations.
When evaluating how a product or service fits into everyday life.
When in-person observation is impractical or too intrusive, for example with private or sensitive topics such as health or finances.
howToDoIt: Define the research goal: Identify the topic, timeframe, and what type of experiences or behaviors participants should capture.
Recruit participants: Choose people who match your target audience and are willing to consistently record entries over time.
Create prompts and tasks: Write clear prompts and tasks that guide entries. Try using a mix of open-ended questions and specific instructions.
Provide tools and instructions: Give participants an easy way to record entries, such as a journal or online form, along with examples and expectations.
Monitor the study: Start the journaling period and stay engaged with participants. Answer any questions, and be sure to check in regularly to monitor participation and reduce incomplete entries.
Collect and organize entries: Sort all entries in a structured way, such as grouping by participant, date, or type of activity. Ensure that everything is complete and easy to navigate when reviewing.
Analyze the data: Review entries and look for recurring themes and patterns across time and participants. Turn these insights into conclusions that inform design decisions.
tips: Keep prompts simple so participants don't feel overwhelmed. Clear, concise questions will lead to more consistent and insightful responses.
Encourage honest responses by reminding participants that there is no right answer. The real, everyday experiences are most valuable and have given the most insight.
Use regular reminders such as texts or emails to help participants stay on track, especially in longer studies where motivation may drop over time.
Combine with follow-up interviews to dig deeper into patterns you notice. The interviews will help explain the "why" behind behaviors documented in the journal entries.
mistakes: Overloading participants with too many prompts or asking for lengthy entries can lead to burnout and participants dropping out before the study ends.

Giving vague or overly complex instructions can lead to participants not fully understanding what to record or how to do it. This could lead to their entries becoming inconsistent or unusable. Try to keep directions simple and easy to follow.

Don't collect data without a clear analysis plan. Diary studies can generate large amounts of unstructured data, and without a plan for organizing and analyzing it, the information can become overwhelming and difficult to use.
Failing to plan for missing or incomplete data can weaken your findings and create gaps in your data. Participants may skip entries or forget to record details.
methods.example: A fitness app wants to understand why users stop using their app after the first few weeks of signing up. They conduct a diary study lasting 2 weeks where participants record each workout, including the activity type, activity duration, what features of the app they used, and how they felt before and after each session. Multiple participants noted that they feel more motivated on days when they see progress tracking or reminders. These entries help the company understand both the specific emotional and situational reasons behind it, which lead to app improvements aimed at user retention.
sources: Martin, B., & Hanington, B. (2012). Universal methods of design: 100 ways to research complex problems, develop innovative ideas, and design effective solutions. Rockport Publishers.
Nielsen Norman Group. (n.d.). Diary studies: Understanding long-term user behavior and experiences. https://www.nngroup.com/articles/diary-studies/
Stephens, G. C., Ottrey, E., & Matthews, K. (2026). A practical guide to using diary methods in qualitative research. Anatomical sciences education, 19(2), 231-241. https://doi.org/10.1002/ase.70102

methods.name: Directed Storytelling
methods.whatItIs: A facilitator uses targeted prompts to guide participants through a first-person account of a specific experience. The structure keeps the story on topic while preserving the richness and sequence of the participant's own telling.
methods.reference: Martin, B., & Hanington, B. (2012). Universal methods of design. Rockport Publishers. Method 31, p. 68.
sources: Martin, B., & Hanington, B. (2012). Universal methods of design. Rockport Publishers. Method 31, p. 68.

methods.name: Ergonomic Analysis
methods.whatItIs: Tools, workstations, and environments are assessed against human physical capability to evaluate fit, reach, posture, effort, and safety. The output is a set of dimensional and configurational requirements grounded in anthropometric data.
methods.reference: Martin, B., & Hanington, B. (2012). Universal methods of design. Rockport Publishers. Method 33, p. 72.
sources: Martin, B., & Hanington, B. (2012). Universal methods of design. Rockport Publishers. Method 33, p. 72.

methods.name: Evidence-Based Design
methods.whatItIs: Design decisions are justified with findings from systematic reviews, published studies, and measured outcomes rather than precedent or preference. The approach is well established in healthcare and education, where decisions carry measurable consequences.
methods.reference: Martin, B., & Hanington, B. (2012). Universal methods of design. Rockport Publishers. Method 35, p. 76.
sources: Martin, B., & Hanington, B. (2012). Universal methods of design. Rockport Publishers. Method 35, p. 76.

methods.name: Experience Sampling Method
methods.whatItIs: Participants are prompted at random intervals to record what they are doing, thinking, or feeling at that moment. Capturing experience in the moment avoids the distortion that creeps into recall after the fact.
methods.reference: Martin, B., & Hanington, B. (2012). Universal methods of design. Rockport Publishers. Method 37, p. 80.
sources: Martin, B., & Hanington, B. (2012). Universal methods of design. Rockport Publishers. Method 37, p. 80.

methods.name: Experiments
methods.whatItIs: Variables are deliberately manipulated under controlled conditions to test whether a specific change produces a specific effect. Experiments answer causal questions that observational methods can only suggest.
methods.reference: Martin, B., & Hanington, B. (2012). Universal methods of design. Rockport Publishers. Method 38, p. 82.
sources: Martin, B., & Hanington, B. (2012). Universal methods of design. Rockport Publishers. Method 38, p. 82.

methods.name: Extremes and Mainstreams

library.book: The Field Guide to Human-Centered Design (IDEO.org, 2015)
library.title: Extremes and Mainstreams

methods.whatItIs: Researchers deliberately recruit people at the edges of a user population alongside typical users. Extreme users make latent needs visible because they have already invented workarounds that mainstream users tolerate silently.
methods.reference: IDEO.org. (2015). The field guide to human-centered design. IDEO.org. Page 49.
sources: IDEO.org. (2015). The field guide to human-centered design. IDEO.org. Page 49.

methods.name: Fly-on-the-Wall Observation
methods.whatItIs: The researcher observes behavior in a natural setting without interacting with participants or altering the situation. Because nothing is asked, nothing is performed, which makes the method useful for establishing a baseline of ordinary behavior.
methods.reference: Martin, B., & Hanington, B. (2012). Universal methods of design. Rockport Publishers. Method 42, p. 90.
sources: Martin, B., & Hanington, B. (2012). Universal methods of design. Rockport Publishers. Method 42, p. 90.

methods.name: Focus Groups
methods.whatItIs: A moderator guides a small, carefully composed group through a structured discussion. The value lies in the interaction between participants, where agreement, disagreement, and elaboration reveal shared language and contested assumptions.
methods.reference: Martin, B., & Hanington, B. (2012). Universal methods of design. Rockport Publishers. Method 43, p. 92.
sources: Martin, B., & Hanington, B. (2012). Universal methods of design. Rockport Publishers. Method 43, p. 92.

methods.name: Graffiti Walls
methods.whatItIs: A public, low-barrier surface such as a poster or whiteboard invites anonymous written and drawn responses to an open prompt. Anonymity and informality lower the cost of participation and surface candid opinion.
methods.reference: Martin, B., & Hanington, B. (2012). Universal methods of design. Rockport Publishers. Method 45, p. 96.
sources: Martin, B., & Hanington, B. (2012). Universal methods of design. Rockport Publishers. Method 45, p. 96.

methods.name: Guerilla User Research

library.book: The User Experience Team of One (Buley, 2013)
library.title: Guerilla User Research

methods.whatItIs: Short, opportunistic sessions conducted in public places gather quick feedback from whoever is available. Rigor is traded for speed and cost, which makes it suited to early directional questions rather than conclusive findings.
methods.reference: Buley, L. (2013). The user experience team of one: A research and design survival guide. Rosenfeld Media. Page 126.
sources: Buley, L. (2013). The user experience team of one: A research and design survival guide. Rosenfeld Media. Page 126.

methods.name: Innovation Sourcebook
methods.whatItIs: Successful offerings, organizations, and practices are collected into a structured, comparable reference library. Organizing examples by shared attributes makes transferable patterns visible across unrelated domains.
methods.reference: Kumar, V. (2013). 101 design methods: A structured approach for driving innovation in your organization. Wiley. Method 1.4.
sources: Kumar, V. (2013). 101 design methods: A structured approach for driving innovation in your organization. Wiley. Method 1.4.

methods.name: Interviews
methods.imageAlt: Two men sit facing each other at a small table during an interview.

library.book: The Field Guide to Human-Centered Design (IDEO.org, 2015)
library.title: Interview

methods.whatItIs: Interviews are a fundamental research method that collect firsthand personal accounts to learn about and understand the people that your design is being created for. Information collected from interviews will help to verify previously gathered data as well as put data into context regarding how your design will cause improvements.
whenToUse: When you need to understand how participants experience scenarios and activities you're designing for.
When you need a deeper level of knowledge of the field where there are users with expertise.
Early in the research phase when you still have an unclear source to the issue.
When you need to learn what users want or need from the product/for their business.
howToDoIt: Define what goal you want to reach from the interview. Identify the topics you want to focus on and determine if the interview should have a loose guide to follow or strict rigid questions to ask participants. Questions should remain open-ended to allow more insight from answers.

Find participants that represent your target users. Interviews may be conducted individually or in organized group settings that allow for users to give answers that more directly answer and expand upon your questions.

Schedule contextual sessions to meet with participants in spaces relevant to the topic. Interviewing participants in a space they are comfortable with or where the activities actually happen allow them to stay on topic and provide better examples for the questions.
Start with broad questions. Asking about the person's life, values, and habits allows them to feel comfortable before you ask more specific questions directly related to the topic.

Take detailed notes and photos. Knowing exactly what the person says is important to understanding and reviewing the information later. The person's body language and surroundings can also give important context and data for the questions.

Debrief immediately with your team. Review the answers gathered from the participant and add notes of your thoughts, questions, and observations that were created during the interview. If you are working with a team, everyone should discuss their thoughts.
whatYouNeed: Permission and consent forms for the interview and photography
Notebook or laptop for detailed answers and notes
Camera or smartphone for photos and videos (if permitted)
1-2 researchers (one to lead, one to document)
Loose or structured interview guide with open-ended questions
tips: Record quotes of what participants answer so their words will not be lost.
Pay attention to body language and how the user interacts with their surroundings, what they say may differ from how they act.
Ask "why" questions and questions about specific occurrences, "Tell me about the last time you ___", rather than what a user "usually" does to understand their motivations and thought process.
Allow room for silence so that participants may think on their answers and give deeper responses.
mistakes: Asking leading questions ("Do you think it's better to…?") instead of focusing on the users unbiased thoughts.
Asking limiting "yes" or "no" questions instead of open ended questions.
Using terms or phrases that may be unclear and interpreted or understood differently.
Interviewing in a mixed group that leads to some participants answering differently due to other participants involved.
Asking questions to confirm assumptions instead of exploring the participant's thoughts.
methods.example: The World Bank's Consultative Group to Assist the Poor (CGAP) and the bank Bancomer wanted to identify opportunities to help low-income Mexicans have better accessibility in saving money. The team conducted interviews with various Mexicans to learn and understand how they saved money, but were often told "I don't save money." As the team asked more questions to understand the people's lives, they learned that many low-income Mexicans used unconventional methods to hold onto money and save it for specific things. One man stashed extra money into his shirt pockets when hanging them up in his closet, while another man would save up money in bricks with the goal to one day buy building supplies and construct a house. The insight that was brought from these methods led the team to design a project-based approach to savings.

methods.name: Laddering
methods.whatItIs: A sequence of why questions moves an interview from concrete product attributes up to the personal values behind them. The resulting chain connects a surface preference to the underlying motivation that drives it.

methods.name: Listening Tour
methods.imageAlt: A woman holding a tablet stands and talks with colleagues seated around a conference table in a bright office.

library.book: The User Experience Team of One (Buley, 2013)
library.title: Listening Tour

methods.whatItIs: A listening tour is a series of conversations in which a leader gathers feedback from employees or stakeholders to identify issues and challenges. It builds trust and understanding, especially when a leader is new or an organization is changing.
whenToUse: When a leader takes a new role, so employees learn who is leading them and the leader learns what matters to them.
When change occurs in an organization or team.
When you are joining a new community.
In the early stage of a design project, to understand what users will need from the design.
When you want to learn people's perspectives on an idea or a pending decision.
When you want to build relationships and trust within a workspace.
When existing feedback channels are not working.
howToDoIt: Define the purpose: Decide what you want to learn and what you will do with the information you collect.
Choose participants: Include a cross-section of roles, units, and locations. Prepare a list of participants and schedule the conversations.
Prepare materials: Write interview prompts, prepare consent forms, and plan how you will record notes.

Set the format: Combine one-on-one conversations with small group sessions. Meet in person when possible, and keep managers and colleagues out of one-on-one conversations so people can speak candidly.

Listen: Open each conversation with a question the group can answer easily. Reassure participants that there are no wrong answers, and pay attention to how people talk and show emotion when they raise problems.
Synthesize: Group your notes into themes, for example with affinity mapping on sticky notes or a virtual whiteboard.
Report back and act: Share what you heard with participants, explain the actions you will take, and keep them updated.
whatYouNeed: Consent forms are one of the main items needed for listening tours- allows everything to be consensual
Interview prompts, questions within the group
Planning, stakeholder, schedules, list of participants
Personal items- notebooks, sticky notes, pens
tips: Start the conversation with a question that is easy for the group to answer.
Do not go directly to a solution. Listen to the team and focus on the problem raised most often.
Be organized, and bring plenty of ideas and questions that will help solve the problem.
Pay close attention to how people talk and show their emotions when they raise problems.
Create psychological safety by assuring participants that their input will be used constructively.
mistakes: Talking too much.
Asking leading questions instead of straightforward ones.
Proposing solutions too early.
Not speaking to everyone in the room.
Responding poorly to people or taking too few notes.
Failing to report back or act on what you hear, which erodes trust.
methods.example: NC State wants to redesign the study rooms in D.H. Hill Library, which students find dark and gloomy. The design team holds a listening tour with students who use the rooms. Participants say they want the rooms to feel safer and more comforting, and the team responds with softer lighting, warm-colored flooring, aesthetic pictures, and better soundproofing.

methods.name: Literature Reviews
methods.imageAlt: Funnel diagram for a literature review that narrows from background and importance, to prior research, to a specific area, to current ideas, to key research questions.
methods.whatItIs: A literature review gathers and analyzes information from published sources and captures the essence of previous research findings, so you can learn more about your research problem. By reviewing the literature, you make connections and become well informed in your area of interest.
whenToUse: When you are starting a research project and need to inform yourself about the topic through other researchers' findings.
When you need to support or defend an argument about the research topic.
When you need to find gaps in your topic that call for further research.
howToDoIt: Choose the topic you want to research and narrow it down.
Decide which type of literature review fits your purpose: chronological, historical, thematic, methodological, theoretical, or meta-analysis.
Explain why the topic is important and what has already been found about it.
Cluster your readings and decide which sources are credible enough for your findings.
Identify any misunderstandings, themes, or gaps that need more research.
Write your final review, stating the topic, naming the gaps, and supporting your findings.
whatYouNeed: A way to keep your connections clear and organized, such as a notebook or a Google Doc
A system for organizing sources, such as Zotero
Plenty of time, so you do not rush
tips: Add your own understanding of the sources instead of only paraphrasing other researchers.
Make connections and use transitions between sources.
Write findings that state a clear connection.
Connect the review to your topic statement so the question is answered.
Include your own perspective on the readings to create added discussion.
Choose good sources.
mistakes: Summarizing the sources without adding your own analysis of the readings.
Choosing a topic that is too broad.
Lacking organization.
Relying on weak sources.
methods.example: An organization wants to advocate for environmental justice. They will assess multiple literature reviews to gather information about human population, air quality, zoning, income disparities. They will compare multiple readings to find the themes, gaps, and areas that need more information. This will help with stating the research topic.

methods.name: Observation
methods.whatItIs: People, artifacts, environments, and interactions are watched and recorded systematically. A defined protocol for what to look at, how to record it, and when to sample separates research observation from casual noticing.
methods.reference: Martin, B., & Hanington, B. (2012). Universal methods of design. Rockport Publishers. Method 57, p. 120.
sources: Martin, B., & Hanington, B. (2012). Universal methods of design. Rockport Publishers. Method 57, p. 120.

methods.name: Participant Observation
methods.whatItIs: Participant observation is an ethnographic method in which the researcher takes part in an activity, setting, or community to understand situations and behaviors from the inside. The researcher joins the life of the participants and records what happens in their setting. Design researchers usually have a more time-limited engagement than anthropologists, but the intent is the same: to form deep connections and empathy with the people being studied and to experience events as they do (Martin & Hanington, 2012).
whenToUse: When you want to understand why people do what they do in their day-to-day lives.
When you are studying how people interact with each other, or the behaviors of a culture or subculture.
When you want empathy built through firsthand experience of an activity rather than secondhand reports.
When you can combine observation with interviews and other ethnographic methods.
howToDoIt: Define a specific research question: Decide which behaviors, interactions, or experiences you want to understand.

Identify participants and a level of participation: Choose the community or activity you will join. Marginal participants blend in as natural observers, for example by riding the bus with commuters. Full participants become members of the group, which design researchers rarely do because of ethical concerns and the time involved.

Plan and prepare: Arrange permissions and legal agreements, and set up your recording tools, such as field notes, a camera, or an audio recorder. A framework such as AEIOU can organize what you notice.

Conduct observations: Take part in the activity while you systematically record the environment, behaviors, interactions, language, motivations, and perceptions of the participants. Ask questions about their environment as you go.
Reflect and follow up: Debrief soon after each session, review your notes, and write a summary. Follow up with interviews or other methods to check what you saw.
whatYouNeed: Enough time in the setting to build trust
tips: Blend in with your environment. Do not talk all the time; observe.
Record and take pictures of everything, and ask obvious questions.
Debrief, follow up, and reflect on your notes as soon as you can.
Combine participant observation with interviews to learn the motivations behind what you see.
mistakes: Paying more attention to your recording tools than to the world you are recording.
Over-documenting or under-documenting. Balance observing and documenting.
Staying in one place instead of moving through the setting.
Jumping in and changing how people operate in their environment instead of letting events play out.
Losing objectivity or influencing the participants' behavior.
methods.example:
Two researchers travel to Cuba to learn how people behave during the current crisis. Instead of staying in a hotel, each researcher stays with someone living through the crisis and joins their daily routine. They ask questions about the environment, use the AEIOU method to organize their notes, and write a summary at the end of each day.

In a marginal form of the method, a service design team rides the bus alongside commuters to observe how riders behave and interact (Martin & Hanington, 2012).

methods.name: Participatory Action Research
methods.whatItIs: The people affected by a problem participate as co-researchers rather than as subjects, sharing authority over questions, analysis, and action. The method is committed to producing change in the setting studied, not only knowledge about it.
methods.reference: Martin, B., & Hanington, B. (2012). Universal methods of design. Rockport Publishers. Method 60, p. 126.
sources: Martin, B., & Hanington, B. (2012). Universal methods of design. Rockport Publishers. Method 60, p. 126.

methods.name: Personal Inventories
methods.imageAlt: Large poster of photographs of sneakers and people linked by diagrams and notes.
methods.whatItIs: Personal inventories document a user's relationship with a physical or digital object and how the user interacts with it in daily life.
whenToUse: When you want to understand a user's lifestyle and needs so you can create designs that are more useful to them.
When you want to find design gaps or pain points so you can identify the root problem and fill the gap.
When you are doing an in-home visit, where you can see how objects are used in context and gain insight into the user's habits.
howToDoIt: Define your goals: Decide which object or user interaction you want to see, and whether you are designing something new or filling gaps and pain points.
Prepare the setup: Decide how users will interact with the objects, whether through a prompted interaction or an at-home visit, and how you will document those interactions.
Conduct the session: Document how users interact with the objects. Ask about their experience and how they feel.
Analyze findings: Look for recurring themes or behaviors, gaps, and pain points.
Synthesize research: Use the data to continue the design process, for example by creating a persona based on your findings.
whatYouNeed: Consent from different users to document and observe
Variety of different objects and tasks for the user to interact with
2-3 researchers to ask questions, facilitate, and document
Camera or video camera to document with (with permission)
Notebook to write down any findings and answers to interview questions
Transportation to users house or transportation for users to testing site
tips: Ask questions. They give you an in-depth understanding of the object.
Keep questions open-ended to get the most authentic user experience.
Make sure users know there is no right or wrong way to interact with the object, and that you are testing the object, not them.
Focus on empathizing with the user, especially if they tell you they struggle with an object daily.
mistakes: Falling into confirmation bias by focusing on your own experience of the object instead of the user's.
Treating qualitative data from the research as quantitative data.
Not documenting enough during the research, and letting your own bias fill the gaps.
methods.example: A designing group wants to design office supplies that are more accessible for people who experience arthritis and other joint related disabilities. The group of researchers interview and test on different people who experience joint disabilities, by asking them to interact with common office supplies and ask them questions on how they navigate using these common supplies with their disability.

methods.name: Photo Studies
methods.whatItIs: Photographs document a setting, or participants photograph their own daily lives in response to a prompt. Participant-taken images reveal what people consider significant enough to record, which is itself a finding.

methods.name: Picture Cards
methods.whatItIs: A curated set of images and words gives participants concrete material to think and talk with. Visual prompts help people describe experiences that are difficult to articulate from memory alone.

methods.name: Popular Media Scan
methods.whatItIs: News, advertising, social platforms, and entertainment are reviewed systematically to identify new language, attitudes, and cultural shifts around a topic. The scan situates a design problem in the public conversation surrounding it.

methods.name: Questionnaires / Surveys
methods.imageAlt: Person typing on a laptop that displays an online survey form.
methods.whatItIs: Questionnaires and surveys are research methods that collect self-reported information from people about their thoughts, behaviors, attitudes, or anything else that is relevant to the study being conducted. This research method is good for producing a large, versatile amount of data in a short time frame.
whenToUse: When you need to gauge a wide range of people's opinions on a research topic before a project is started.
When you need to gather feedback after a prototyping session.
When you need to collect current consumer preferences when researching for a new product.
howToDoIt: Identify the topic of your research and decide whether a survey would further it.
Create questions for the survey. Think about what information would be most useful to gather for the project.
Identify the demographic for the survey: decide whom you will collect data from.
Send out the survey to a group of respondents.
Gather the results after enough surveys are completed and compile it into qualitative and quantitative research data.
Use the data collected for analysis in the insights phase.
whatYouNeed: Digital survey: survey creation tool (ex Google forms), email or other method of distribution
Physical survey: paper, markers, glue, tape, location for display
tips: Keep questions short and straightforward.
Ask one thing at a time to avoid double-barrelled questions.
Avoid leading questions that lead respondents to picking a certain answer due to a bias.
mistakes: Sometimes surveys can be inaccurate or not reflect true feelings or opinions of users. Researchers should try their best to avoid or recognize biases.
Know the difference: questionnaires are sets of specific questions within surveys, while surveys describe the broader scope of the data collection process.
methods.example: A researcher wants to redesign the UI of a self checkout kiosk at a grocery store. They decide to provide a survey to customers at the store to gauge satisfaction with the current UI by providing it at the end of every transaction that is completed. After a few weeks of gathering results, the researcher gathers the data and notices that customers are reporting on the question "Did you have any problems during your experience?" that they had issues with the kiosk detecting items in the bagging area when there are none. The researcher uses this result to begin designing an improved kiosk that fixes this issue to improve customer experience.

methods.name: Remote Moderated Research
methods.whatItIs: A researcher observes and converses with a participant in real time while that participant uses their own device in their own setting. It preserves much of the dialogue of an in-person session while widening geographic reach.
methods.reference: Martin, B., & Hanington, B. (2012). Universal methods of design. Rockport Publishers. Method 69, p. 144.

methods.name: Secondary Research

library.book: The Field Guide to Human-Centered Design (IDEO.org, 2015)
library.title: Secondary Research

methods.whatItIs: Existing studies, reports, datasets, and documentation are gathered and synthesized before any new data is collected. Done first, it prevents a team from spending primary research effort on questions that are already answered.

methods.name: Semantic Differential
methods.whatItIs: Participants rate a concept on a series of bipolar adjective scales, such as cluttered to clean. The resulting profile turns aesthetic and emotional response into comparable quantitative data.

methods.name: Shadowing
methods.imageAlt: AI-generated image of a student holding a clipboard and observing a nurse who adjusts an IV pole in a hospital room.
methods.imageSource: ChatGPT, using the prompt: Generate an image of a student with a clipboard observing a nurse working in the hospital
methods.whatItIs: Shadowing is a research method in which designers closely follow and observe users in their natural environment as they complete everyday tasks or interact with a product, service, or space. It yields real-world insight into behaviors, challenges, routines, and unmet needs. Because it is exploratory, it builds baseline familiarity with a user group and may suggest early design implications (Martin & Hanington, 2012).
whenToUse: When you want to discover barriers or pain points that would not normally appear in an interview or an online review.
When you want to expose what is causing a problem and where it went wrong, rather than only analyzing what is wrong.
When you need baseline familiarity with a user group early in a project.
howToDoIt: Identify the research goal and the behaviors, tasks, or interactions you want to observe.
Select participants who regularly use the product, service, or environment being studied, and obtain their cooperation and any needed clearances.
Observe and follow participants, at a respectful distance, as they move through their tasks or environments.
Record notes on actions, behaviors, obstacles, and interactions with people or objects. Photographs, sketches, and audio can add detail.
Analyze patterns and recurring or unexpected challenges.
Reflect on the findings and how they can become design opportunities, recommendations, or improvements.
whatYouNeed: A clipboard or notebook and a writing utensil
A camera or audio recorder, where permitted
Permission from the person you shadow and any needed clearances
tips: Analyze the intentionality of the process and the order of steps.
Time certain activities and observe why and how they take that long.
Observe the same person doing the same task at different times to see whether the order or challenges stay consistent.
Have several team members shadow different representative users to build a general picture of patterns.
mistakes: Interfering with the natural process of how the activity plays out.
Rushing the person being watched. The process can be time-consuming.
Following people without their knowledge or consent in settings where cooperation is needed.
methods.example: A healthcare design team shadows a nurse during a hospital shift to observe how they move through patient rooms, access medical supplies, doors and other equipment. Researchers take into account the long distances walked to retrieve equipment and the frequent interruptions on the way. This information allows the team to redesign the supply station layout and system to better support the efficiency of the workflow in such a high stakes environment as this one.

methods.name: Triading
methods.whatItIs: Participants are shown three items and asked how two are alike and different from the third. The distinctions they volunteer expose the personal criteria they use to categorize, without the researcher supplying the categories.

methods.name: Unobtrusive Measures
methods.whatItIs: Unobtrusive measures are ways of gathering information without direct contact with participants, so the researcher does not intrude on the research context. They draw on physical traces, archival records, and nonintrusive observation. The measures were proposed in the late 1960s in response to the bias built into self-report and direct-contact methods such as surveys and interviews (Martin & Hanington, 2012).
whenToUse: When you are researching a sensitive topic.
When you want to observe natural behavior without participants changing it, including avoiding the Hawthorne effect.
When self-report methods such as surveys and interviews are likely to produce biased answers.
When physical evidence, records, or recordings of events that have already occurred are available.
howToDoIt: Formulate a research question: Determine what behavior or social pattern you need to study without direct interference.

Select a type of measure: Choose among physical traces (erosion measures such as worn tiles or paths, and accretion measures such as litter or graffiti), archival records (public documents, social media, historical records, traffic counters), and observation of behavior in public settings without interaction.
Identify data sources: Find relevant sources, such as public records, library records, or physical evidence in public spaces.
Collect and analyze data: Measure the traces or analyze the records. For instance, you could check car radio settings in a garage to estimate radio station popularity.

Check ethical boundaries: Confirm that the behaviors or records are publicly accessible. Collecting clues without participants' knowledge raises questions about consent and privacy, so plan for them before you collect anything.
Triangulate and validate: Compare findings across multiple types of data and with other research methods. Unobtrusive measures should not be used in isolation.
whatYouNeed: A research question that traces, records, or observations can answer
Access to public records, archives, or public spaces
A camera and notebook to document physical evidence
A spreadsheet or coding sheet to log what you find
Other research methods to triangulate your findings
tips: Do not interact with participants, but you can change what they interact with.
Look for both kinds of physical trace: wear patterns show preferred paths and heavily used features, while litter, graffiti, and makeshift signs point to shortcomings in a design.
Digital footprints, such as wireless network names and locations, can also serve as traces of technology use.
Be creative about data sources. The measures are meant to be flexible and to draw on unusual sources.
mistakes: Assuming the data is complete. Common drawbacks are limited validity, limited data availability, and difficulty accounting for social context.
Overlooking ethics. The method involves gathering clues without informed consent, so stay within publicly accessible behaviors and records.
Drawing conclusions without knowing who contributed the data, which is a limitation of the method.
Using the method alone instead of triangulating it with other research.
methods.example:
Designers and urban planners look at dirt paths that pedestrians create by cutting across grass instead of using paved sidewalks. The paths show the most natural, efficient route users want to take, which often leads to redesigning the walkways.

In another case, researchers paired photographs of graffiti, an accretion trace, with other research methods to build awareness of the different viewpoints held by graffiti writers and community members (Martin & Hanington, 2012).

methods.name: Abstraction Laddering
methods.whatItIs: A problem statement is reframed by asking why to move up toward broader purpose and how to move down toward concrete action. Moving deliberately in both directions helps a team find the altitude at which the problem is both meaningful and solvable.
methods.reference: LUMA Institute. (2012). Innovating for people: Handbook of human-centered design methods. LUMA Institute. Page 52.
sources: LUMA Institute. (2012). Innovating for people: Handbook of human-centered design methods. LUMA Institute. Page 52.

methods.name: AEIOU
methods.imageAlt: A woman wearing a wireless earbud looks on with a puzzled expression in a cafe while a barista works behind her.
methods.whatItIs: AEIOU is an observational method that focuses on five areas of a user: activities, environments, interactions, objects, and users. The idea of this method is to gather information from messy observations and transform it into organized information that will help the researcher understand people's needs and problems.
whenToUse: At the beginning of a project, to understand the real-life behavior of a user.
When you observe users in their natural environment, because it helps capture real-world context.
When you need to organize previous data, such as notes, photos, and interviews, into categories.
howToDoIt: Find your goal or question that will guide you through the observation.
Print out an AEIOU worksheet with ample space in each section (5 sections).
Choose a specific place you want to observe.
Watch multiple users interacting with others, the environment or other interactions in the real-world setting and record what you see, hear, and notice.
Use each section in the worksheet to categorize and organize what is being observed.
Cluster patterns that have similar observations (patterns, behaviors, or common issues) and identify the users needs, issues, and positive interactions.
Create ideas that can help improvements to the issues.
tips: Don't guess or anticipate the behavior, just watch it. People may act different than they say.
Use the worksheet during the observation to guide what you pay attention to.
Give as much detail as you can from each interaction, record to capture multiple angles.
Connect the observations between sections.
Work with others to get as much observation insights as possible.
mistakes: Filling in the worksheet only at the end, which can make insights shallow. AEIOU is a tool, but it is also a path the researcher creates to find as many insights as possible.
Focusing only on the user and ignoring the environment, objects, and interactions.
Isolating the sections, which blinds the researcher to the influence the sections have on one another.
Making assumptions instead of finding new ideas that develop the analysis.
Jumping to conclusions. The method alone can miss why behavior happens, so integrate other research methods.
methods.example:
A researcher walks around a grocery store and observes groups of shoppers. Under Activities, the researcher records, "the customer picks up an item and reads the ingredients on the back of the box." Under Environments: "some customers seem to be sensitive to the bright lights inside the store." Under Interactions: "multiple customers find staff and ask them questions about items and item placement," plus interactions at checkout, whether at the self-checkout or a regular register. Under Objects: groceries, carts, baskets, self-checkout kiosks, and pin pads. Under Users: a mom and son, an older couple, teenagers coming from the gym, and staff.

These observations help the researcher understand that the environment can affect users' mood ("too many people in one aisle can overwhelm an older couple shopping") and that objects can be a barrier to a successful shopping trip ("the pin pad constantly messes up, and the self-checkout is complicated to use").

methods.name: Affinity Diagramming
methods.whatItIs: Observations, quotes, and findings are written individually and clustered by similarity until themes stabilize. Because grouping precedes labeling, the categories come from the data rather than from the team's prior expectations.
methods.reference: Martin, B., & Hanington, B. (2012). Universal methods of design. Rockport Publishers. Method 3, p. 12.
sources: Martin, B., & Hanington, B. (2012). Universal methods of design. Rockport Publishers. Method 3, p. 12.

methods.name: Bull's-eye Diagramming
methods.imageAlt: Bull's-eye diagram of three concentric rings labeled First, Second, and Third, with sticky notes placed in each ring and two ideas in the center.
methods.whatItIs: A visual method of organizing research's findings by placing them in a concentric circle based on importance. This produces a prioritized view of insights to help teams more quickly identify what is most relevant.
whenToUse: When you need to find an order of importance after data collection.
When you are comparing multiple insights to determine their impact.
When the team needs direction toward the focus of the problem.
When you are preparing research for ideation.
When you want to simplify complex data into a clear visual hierarchy.
howToDoIt: Define your criteria: Decide what the center represents, such as highest user importance, and make sure the team agrees on that definition before starting.
Draw the diagram: Draw a set of concentric circles on a whiteboard or large paper to represent levels of importance.
Prepare the insights: Write each insight or observation on a separate sticky note, keeping each one concise and specific.
Place high-priority insights: Start by placing the most critical insights in the center circle, based on your criteria.
Sort the remaining insights: Continue placing the other insights in the outer rings according to their level of importance.
Discuss and adjust: Debate placements as a team, move items, and refine priorities.
Label and reflect: Add labels if needed, then step back to identify patterns, clusters, or gaps that can inform the next methods.
tips: Clearly define what "priority" means before starting.
Keep insights short and easy to understand.
Encourage discussion to build a shared understanding.
Step back to look for patterns after organizing.
Let the diagram drive decisions rather than just displaying information.
mistakes: Vague or inconsistent criteria for placing insights.
Overcrowding the diagram with too many items.
Letting one person decide placements without team input.
Treating all insights as equally important.
Not revisiting the diagram when new insights arise.
methods.example: A team redesigning a campus dining experience analyzes student feedback from surveys and interviews. They use the Bull's-eye Diagramming method to prioritize insights such as "wait times, dietary restrictions, and unclear labeling". By placing "wait times" at the center, the team identifies it as the most critical issue affecting user experience. This clarity helps them focus their ideation efforts towards improving speed before addressing secondary issues.
sources: Vibe. (n.d.). Bull's eye diagram: What they are & how to make them. https://vibe.us/blog/bulls-eye-diagram/

Hanington, B., & Martin, B. (2019). Universal methods of design, expanded and revised. Rockport Publishers.

methods.name: Card Sorting
methods.imageAlt: Student places green sticky notes with food drawings under category headings such as breakfast and lunch on a wall.

library.book: The Field Guide to Human-Centered Design (IDEO.org, 2015)
library.title: Card Sort

methods.whatItIs: Card sorting is a user research method where participants organize the cards into groups that make sense to them, helping reveal how people naturally structure and interpret information. It produces insights into users mental pathing and can produce potential ways to organize information in a way that makes sense to the user.
whenToUse: When you are designing or restructuring a website or app navigation interface.
When you are organizing large, complex sets of content where grouping is unclear or debated.
When you want to understand how users mentally group information.
When you are validating an existing structure to see if users understand or agree with it.
When you are improving search and filter systems so users can locate content more quickly.
howToDoIt: Define the research goal: Identify what you are trying to learn. A clear goal helps determine how many cards you need and who to recruit.

Create and prepare the cards: Break your content into small, clear, and meaningful items. Each card should represent one image, word, or concept. Avoid vague, overly technical, or unclear wording and imagery so participants can easily understand each item.

Recruit the right participants: Select participants who match your target users as closely as possible. Aim for around 15 participants for qualitative insights. After 15 participants, there are diminishing insights that can be gathered from the card sort.

Explain the task clearly to participants: Give simple instructions such as: "group these cards in a way that makes sense to you." Emphasize that there are no right or wrong answers. Also ask them to label their groups after sorting and explain their decisions.

Observe and document the process: Without influencing them, watch how participants think and group items. Take notes on confusion/hesitation or unique groupings. Ask follow-up questions like why they grouped certain items together, and record answers.

Analyze patterns and identify themes: After collecting all sessions, look for repeated groupings across participants. Identify common category names and outliers. Use this data to refine your information structure and organize your information in a way that is more natural for your user.
whatYouNeed: Recording method (notes, video recorder, audio recorder)
tips: Avoid leading participants toward any "correct" structure. Let them interpret the cards freely, so the results reflect their real mental thought process.
Replace technical jargon with terms your users would actually recognize. If participants don't understand a card, the data becomes unreliable.
Aim for a balanced set (often 30-60 items depending on complexity) so users can sort without fatigue. Too many cards can overwhelm participants.
Asking participants to think out loud and explain their reasoning can reveal valuable insights about how they interpret and group information.
Don't overreact to individual outliers, as one unusual grouping isn't necessarily a problem. Rather, focus on patterns across multiple participants.
mistakes: Writing cards with vague terms can confuse participants and lead to unreliable groupings. Every card should represent one clear, specific idea, word, or image that the user understands.
Only recording how cards are grouped without asking why can lead to unclear insights. The "why" often explains surprising or inconsistent patterns.
Treating card sorting as a final solution instead of a guide, as it does not automatically produce the perfect navigation system. Some further interpretation and iteration are always needed.
Using participants who are not your target audience can result in misleading structures that don't work in real-world use.
methods.example: A healthcare provider is redesigning its patient portal to make it easier for patients to find information like appointment scheduling, billing, test results, and prescription refills. They conduct a card sort with patients using cards labeled with these features, along with others that the patients may need to access. During analysis, the team notices that several participants put "Patient Refills" under the "Medication" category. Based on these patterns, the design team is able to create a more intuitive portal structure that better matches how patients expect to find and manage their healthcare information.

methods.name: Cognitive Mapping
methods.imageAlt: Whiteboard crowded with colorful sticky notes and handwritten arrows linking questions, ideas, and problems.
methods.imageSource: Wikimedia Commons, Chapters Dialogue I, Wikimedia Conference 2014 (Creative Commons license)
methods.whatItIs: Cognitive mapping shows how someone thinks about a topic by turning their thoughts into a visual map. It is most effective for structuring complex problems and informing decisions. The nodes of a cognitive map use the exact words and phrases participants speak, and the links show cause and effect (Martin & Hanington, 2012).
whenToUse: When you want to understand how people see or organize something.
When a topic feels confusing and needs structure.
When you are designing systems, apps, or experiences.
When you are analyzing research or interview notes.
howToDoIt: Pick what you are mapping, such as a concept, process, or experience.
Gather information, such as notes, interviews, and observations.
Write down key ideas or steps, using participants' own words where possible.
Group similar ideas together.
Connect them with lines or arrows.
Look for patterns or gaps.
Clean the map up so it is easy to read.
whatYouNeed: Sticky notes or a digital board (Miro, FigJam)
tips: Do not try to make the map perfect at first.
Focus on how the user thinks.
Pay attention to repeated ideas.
Practice on existing transcripts or recorded interviews before you map in the field.
Combine individual maps into a group map to weave together multiple points of view and build consensus.
mistakes: Organizing too early.
Making it too neat and missing insight.
Ignoring emotions or user feelings.
methods.example: A student maps out their campus experience and realizes feeling "lost" connects to both navigation and making friends. That shows a bigger problem than expected.

methods.name: Concept Mapping
methods.imageAlt: Diagram titled Understanding Concept Maps in which one concept branches into two sub concepts, each linked to two ideas.
methods.imageSource: a graphic published by the Interaction Design Foundation, whose logo appears in the image
methods.whatItIs: Concept mapping is a visual method used to organize ideas by connecting related concepts around a central theme. It helps turn scattered thoughts into a structured understanding and reveals relationships between ideas.
whenToUse: When you are trying to understand a complex topic or problem, especially when ideas feel scattered or unclear.
During brainstorming, to organize thoughts and identify connections between concepts.
When you are preparing for a project or building a framework.
When you want to clarify what you already know and what still needs to be explored.
howToDoIt: Write the main idea or topic in the center of the page.
Add related concepts branching out from the center and connect them with lines or arrows.
Label the relationships when needed and group similar ideas into clusters.
Expand the map by adding more detailed sub-points.
Review and reorganize the map to improve its clarity and structure.
whatYouNeed: Digital tools such as Miro, Lucidchart, or Google Drawings (optional)
tips: Keep the map simple and avoid overcrowding it with too many ideas at once.
Focus on showing connections between concepts rather than only listing information.
Use clear labels so the relationships are easy to understand.
mistakes: Making the map too linear. It should remain flexible and open.
Trying to make the map perfect on the first attempt. It is acceptable to revise and reorganize.
methods.example: For a project on improving a college campus app, a student creates a concept map starting with "User Experience" in the center. They branch out into areas like navigation, design, and accessibility, then add smaller ideas under each category. This helps them see how different features are connected and identify which areas need the most improvement.
sources: Cornell University, Learning Strategies Center. (n.d.). Concept mapping. https://lsc.cornell.edu/how-to-study/concept-maps/
Novak, J. D. (2010). Learning, creating, and using knowledge: Concept maps as facilitative tools in schools and corporations. Routledge.
