methods.name: Content Analysis
methods.imageAlt: Colleagues seated at a table with laptops while a woman points to rows of sticky notes on a wall.
methods.whatItIs: Content analysis is a method for analyzing existing media, text, and images. During analysis, you search for common patterns, themes, and meanings behind the materials you have found.
whenToUse: When you are analyzing existing content, such as images, text, and videos from the past, to find the meaning behind it.
When you want to learn about an old baseball team from 1970s flyers.
When you want to learn about players on an NFL team from images posted on social media.
When you want to learn how two separate groups communicate for work purposes.
howToDoIt: Define a research question: Before analyzing any data, decide what you need to identify and which materials you will study.
Choose a sample: Select the set of content to analyze. The sample size should match what the research question needs to answer.
Develop a coding framework: Create a clear, straightforward set of categories for marking the content.
Test and refine: Try the framework on part of the sample, then adjust the categories to fit what you are studying.
Label the content: Go through all of the content and assign each item to a category in an organized way.
Study the patterns: Find and label the patterns across the coded content to make the design solution easier to see.
Synthesize insights: Once the content is coded and analyzed, identify a design direction that works with all of the data.
tips: Keep all coding categories organized.
Find patterns that fit the research, and do not skip important information before placing it in the coding framework.
Analyze qualitative and quantitative results separately, then combine them.
mistakes: Using categories that are too simple to hold accurate information.
Letting personal bias get in the way of the content.
Studying content without background information, which creates bias.
methods.example: A design team analyzes student reviews of a group of teachers and codes the reviews into categories of negative and positive feedback. Reading the patterns within each topic gives the team the insight it needs to redesign the course outline handed out at the start of each year.
sources: Krippendorff, K. (2018). Content analysis: An introduction to its methodology (4th ed.). SAGE Publications.
Neuendorf, K. A. (2017). The content analysis guidebook (2nd ed.). SAGE Publications.
Stemler, S. (2001). An overview of content analysis. Practical Assessment, Research & Evaluation, 7(17).

methods.name: Create Insight Statements

library.book: The Field Guide to Human-Centered Design (IDEO.org, 2015)
library.title: Create Insight Statements

methods.whatItIs: Research themes are distilled into short, declarative sentences that name a tension worth designing for. A strong insight statement is non-obvious, grounded in evidence, and specific enough to generate ideas.
methods.reference: IDEO.org. (2015). The field guide to human-centered design. IDEO.org. Page 81.

methods.name: Elito Method
methods.whatItIs: A structured matrix links observations to interpretations, value judgments, and design consequences in a single traceable row. The format makes the reasoning from evidence to recommendation explicit and reviewable.
methods.reference: Martin, B., & Hanington, B. (2012). Universal methods of design. Rockport Publishers. Method 32, p. 70.
sources: Martin, B., & Hanington, B. (2012). Universal methods of design. Rockport Publishers. Method 32, p. 70.

methods.name: ERAF Systems Diagram
methods.whatItIs: A complex system is modeled by mapping its entities, their relationships, their attributes, and the flows between them. Making structure and exchange visible exposes dependencies and leverage points that narrative description misses.
methods.reference: Kumar, V. (2013). 101 design methods: A structured approach for driving innovation in your organization. Wiley. Method 4.5.

methods.name: Experience Diagramming
methods.imageAlt: LUMA Experience Diagram of a commuter named Claudia, showing the people, places, and things she interacts with during her commute, with a quote under each step.
methods.imageSource: LUMA Institute, Experience Diagramming reference guide
methods.whatItIs: Experience diagramming is a type of user journey mapping where a researcher documents a user's steps, emotions, actions, and interactions during a specific task or set of circumstances. This process is documented in a visual diagram showing key events and points of interest, often organized into sections such as people, places, things, time, etc.
whenToUse: When the situation you need to map is broader than a regular user journey map.
When the researcher needs to understand pain points and places of improvement within a design.
Before a prototype is created, to identify which problems need to be solved by the design.
howToDoIt: Decide the user experience that you want to create a map of.
Observe the experience of one or more users and take notes.
Gather all the necessary information to properly document the experience in a diagram within these notes (steps taken, points of struggle, specific events).
Write out each step in chronological order.
Organize steps and other aspects into a diagram format (flow chart, map, timeline, etc) using paper or a digital tool.
Use the diagram to inform further research or prototyping.
whatYouNeed: Physical diagram: pens, paper, sticky notes, tape, markers
Digital diagram: a digital diagramming/mapping tool of choice (ex Google slides, Lucidchart, Miro)
tips: Diagram more than just the overview of a user's actions, highlight their key decisions and pain points as well as other people who may have been part of the experience.
This method is useful for not only informing design decisions but also deepening your empathy for users.
Study the patterns in the diagram such as common behaviors and actions.
mistakes: Avoid biases: document exactly what happened, do not let personal assumptions influence diagrams.
Keep diagrams neat, straightforward, and easy to read so that other researchers can use them.
methods.example: A researcher wants to streamline the public transportation system in a big US city. They take a day to observe the typical daily commute to and from work of one of their friends. They take notes on things like where this friend gets on the bus, how long she is on, what stop she gets off, how late or on time the bus was, and how long it takes them to arrive at work. They then create an experience diagram showing a timeline of their friend's commute, featuring the locations in the experience, the people they interacted with (ex the bus driver), and the things they needed for the commute (ex a bus pass). The researcher also highlights issues their friend experienced such as the bus being 10 minutes late, and used this diagram to inform their research on how to improve the bus system.

methods.name: Find Themes

library.book: The Field Guide to Human-Centered Design (IDEO.org, 2015)
library.title: Find Themes

methods.whatItIs: Research data is grouped and regrouped until recurring patterns can be named as overarching topics. The step converts a large volume of individual observations into a manageable set of narrative threads.

methods.name: Importance/Difficulty Matrix
methods.whatItIs: Items are plotted on two axes, value returned against effort required. The resulting quadrants give a team a shared, visible basis for sequencing work rather than arguing priority in the abstract.

methods.name: Kano Analysis
methods.whatItIs: Features are classified by how their presence or absence affects satisfaction, separating basic expectations from linear satisfiers and unexpected delighters. The model explains why adding more of a feature sometimes produces no gain at all.

methods.name: KJ Technique
methods.whatItIs: A silent variant of affinity clustering developed by Jiro Kawakita, in which participants group and rank items without speaking. Removing discussion during sorting prevents dominant voices from steering the outcome.
methods.reference: Martin, B., & Hanington, B. (2012). Universal methods of design. Rockport Publishers. Method 49, p. 104.

methods.name: Mental Model Diagrams
methods.imageAlt: Mental model diagram with a row of tasks from getting dressed to commuting, and supporting actions and tools stacked beneath each task.
methods.whatItIs: Visual tools that map out how a person thinks, feels, and behaves (top half) against a company's features, products, or service offerings (the bottom half). This results in a "bottom-up" organized chart that shows the why behind user actions, it helps to justify design decisions during the insights phase.
whenToUse: When you have multiple audience segments that do similar things but accomplish them in different ways, and you need a structured way to synthesize it.
When you need to create a product strategy that resonates with existing human patterns rather than trying to force new behavior.
When you want to move beyond "user personas" to understand the functional and emotional logic behind user actions, and ultimately why people complete tasks the way they do.
When you need to create a long-term strategic roadmap that is grounded in human behavior rather than technical features.
howToDoIt: Identify your "Task Based Audience Segments": Interview at least four people per segment to ensure a representative sample of behaviors rather than just demographics.
Analyze Transcripts or Notes: Find and extract between 60-120 singularly focused building blocks per person. These should be verb-driven statements describing a specific behavior, belief, or emotion.
Group into Towers: Cluster these building blocks together into vertical "towers" that represent a specific pattern or micro-goal.
Create Mental Spaces: Group related towers into larger "mental spaces" that represent broad stages of the user's experience or philosophy ("Planning" or "Executing").
Align the Bottom Half: Place your specific product features or service offerings in the bottom half of the diagram directly under the towers they are designed to support to identify gaps or overlaps.
whatYouNeed: Participants and qualitative data sources, such as interview transcripts or notes
Color-coded sticky notes, physical or digital
A feature list or product roadmap
tips: Focus on verbs. When labeling user tasks, start each label with a verb.
Focus on beliefs. People behave in ways consistent with their beliefs, so capture those and not only physical actions.
Collaborate. Do the initial clustering with a partner to reduce personal bias.
mistakes: Confusing the top and bottom: placing product features in the top half. In this framework, users' behaviors and beliefs go at the top and solutions at the bottom.
Focusing on the tool: mapping how someone uses a specific tool rather than the underlying task they are trying to accomplish, regardless of the tool.
Using a small sample: studying fewer than four people per audience segment, which may lead to an incomplete model.
methods.example: A design team researching student health identifies a task-based audience segment of "Busy Student Athletes" and pulls over 100 different behaviors from each interview transcript. In the top half of the diagram, they group these into "Mental Spaces" like "Nutrition Planning" and "Gym Motivation," with specific towers under "Nutrition Planning" showing thoughts like "calculating macros for a bulk" or "prepping meals for the whole week to save time." In the bottom half, the team maps out their new fitness app's features, like a "Barcode Scanner" and a "Workout Tracker," right under the towers they match with. This actually shows that while the app is great for "tracking calories," there's a huge gap under the "finding cheap healthy food on campus" tower, which means the team needs to add a "Campus Dining Hall Macro-Guide" feature so the app actually works for a student's daily life.

methods.name: Mind Mapping
methods.whatItIs: A central topic branches outward into related concepts in a nonlinear, radiating structure. The format suits early consolidation, when the relationships between ideas matter more than their sequence.

methods.name: Personas
methods.imageAlt: Persona profile for Drew, an influencer, with a portrait of a young man in glasses and sections for about, motivations, core needs, event influencers, and pain points.
methods.imageSource: User Personas: The Complete Guide for UX Designers (With Examples)
methods.whatItIs: Personas are archetypal descriptions of user behavior patterns, distilled into relatable, human profiles.
whenToUse: When you need to understand and empathize with different user types.
When you are designing for a broad or diverse audience with varying needs.
When you are prioritizing features or design decisions based on user needs.
When you are synthesizing interviews, observations, and surveys.
When you need scenarios for how a product or service will be used.
howToDoIt: Collect research from user interviews, surveys, etc.
Identify patterns, behaviors, needs/goals.
Cluster similar users into groups based on characteristics.
Define each group into a persona with different names, demographics, and context.
Describe goals, motivations, behaviors, and pain points.
Add background info and place the users into a scenario involving the product or service.
whatYouNeed: Maps and diagrams synthesizing the data
Creative team for building unique personas
tips: Limit the number of personas to three to five for each project.
Present each persona in a page-length or shorter description.
Base personas on real data from user research.
Keep personas simple and easy to remember.
Update the personas and refer back to them throughout the design process.
mistakes: Basing personas on assumptions and stereotypes.
Making too many personas.
Including details irrelevant to user research.
Not updating the personas as the design process continues.
methods.example: A design team is tasked with creating an app for college students to help manage work. They conduct interviews with students and provide surveys for them to complete. Using the data from them, they create several personas of students with different characteristics, behaviors, and pain points. These personas are then used to help prioritize what features students may need the most in the app.

methods.name: POEMS
methods.imageAlt: Sketch of a researcher capturing observations of users and sorting them into five categories: people, objects, environments, messages, and services.
methods.whatItIs: An observation framework used to categorize elements into 5 different categories (People, Objects, Environments, Messages, and Services) in order to understand how these elements work both independently as well as with other elements as a whole system.
whenToUse: When you want to analyze something in the broader context of its surroundings.
When you want to understand how an element works on its own.
When you want to know why something is the way it is because of the influences around it.
howToDoIt: Prepare: Gather the tools and materials you need for your observations.
Create a template: Make a note-taking sheet organized by the POEMS categories (People, Objects, Environments, Messages, Services).
Enter the field: Go to the setting you are studying. Observe, and talk to people to understand the environment, the objects, and the information they interact with.
Sort your observations: Review your notes and record how each observation relates to a letter in POEMS.
Summarize the context: Describe the overall context your observations reveal, and share it with your team.
whatYouNeed: Enough time for a thorough study
tips: Go to the field at the time most likely to give you the information you need.
If you interview people, try to include a wide range of people present in the field.
Stay as long as you need to take good observation notes.
mistakes: Forgetting materials you may need, which can cost you good information.
Staying in one spot, which limits what you can observe.
Going too early or too late, unless the activity you are studying happens only then, because fewer people will be present.
methods.example: You want to see why people go to a certain amusement park so you go to an amusement park during its busy hours. You observe people having fun on rides, ask people what their favorite things to do there are, and see what locations in the park attract what people.
sources: Crawford, K. (2024, July 8). The Poems Method for user observation/research, template. Atomic Spin. https://spin.atomicobject.com/poems-template-user-observation/
DesignSociety.org. (n.d.). Poems. The Design Society - a worldwide community. https://www.designsociety.org/exchange/method/77/poems
Kumar, V. (2013). 101 design methods: A structured approach for driving innovation in your organization. Wiley.

methods.name: Problem Tree Analysis
methods.whatItIs: A core problem is placed at the trunk, its root causes below and its consequences above. Separating causes from effects keeps a team from designing against a symptom.
methods.reference: LUMA Institute. (2012). Innovating for people: Handbook of human-centered design methods. LUMA Institute. Page 48.
sources: LUMA Institute. (2012). Innovating for people: Handbook of human-centered design methods. LUMA Institute. Page 48.

methods.name: Rose, Thorn, Bud
methods.imageAlt: Green wall with pink, blue, and green sticky notes sorted under headings for app pages such as Home, Deals, and Account.
methods.whatItIs: Rose, Thorn, Bud is an insight method that focuses on categorizing different items as positive (Rose), negative (Thorn), or appearing as a possibility that has yet to be explored (Bud).
whenToUse: When you need to visually see what works well and what works poorly.
For identifying key design opportunities that will enhance the product.
When designers want to review what works in the design concept.
When participants need a way to share their feedback with designers.
howToDoIt: Define your focus: Decide who will participate (designers or participants) and what you will assess: what works, what works poorly, and what needs work in your design.
Assign colors: On sticky notes or a similar format, give Rose, Thorn, and Bud different colors. The colors help distinguish the notes visually and make sorting and examination easier.

Start noting: Without judging responses, write whatever comes to mind about what works well, what works poorly, and what needs work. Place the notes in separate sections of the board for Rose, Thorn, and Bud.
Organize: After about 15 minutes, or once all the notes are complete, organize them beyond the Rose, Thorn, and Bud categories by finding other relationships and connections.
Analyze: Use the organized notes to point out trends and patterns in the design, and decide what should stay and what needs to be removed.
tips: Do not be afraid to be harsh when writing thorns. Candor helps expose deeper issues with the design.
Add simple drawings to notes to support the process.
Include every idea that comes to mind.
mistakes: Writing long, complicated notes, which hinders organization and analysis.
Using the method only once. Consistent, repeated use throughout the design process is more effective for continually identifying issues.
methods.example: A design firm is working on a website interface for a car company. The team is midway through the design process but senses that the website is a little off. Using Rose, Thorn, Bud, the designers run the exercise and produce many insights about the website: some positive, some negative, and some that need more work. They discover many previously unnoticed negative features that, once removed, make the website more navigable for users.
sources: Martin, B., & Hanington, B. (2012). Universal methods of design: 100 ways to research complex problems, develop innovative ideas, and design effective solutions. Rockport Publishers.
Becker, J. (2021). Rose, thorn, bud. Open Practice Library. https://openpracticelibrary.com/practice/rose-thorn-bud/
Crawford, K. (2024, August 12). Rose, bud, thorn (Design thinking activity #9). Atomic Spin. https://spin.atomicobject.com/design-thinking-rose-bud-thorn/

methods.name: Stakeholder Maps
methods.whatItIs: Everyone with an interest in a system is diagrammed along with their relationships, influence, and competing priorities. The map reveals who must be consulted, who can block a decision, and whose needs are currently unrepresented.
methods.reference: Martin, B., & Hanington, B. (2012). Universal methods of design. Rockport Publishers. Method 80, p. 166.
sources: Martin, B., & Hanington, B. (2012). Universal methods of design. Rockport Publishers. Method 80, p. 166.

methods.name: Statement Starters
methods.imageAlt: Four colleagues gather at a whiteboard covered in sticky notes while a woman points to one of the notes.

library.book: The Field Guide to Human-Centered Design (IDEO.org, 2015)
library.title: How Might We

methods.whatItIs: Statement starters, also known as How Might We (HMW) questions, reframe identified problems as open-ended questions so a team can explore a wide range of solutions collaboratively. The phrasing is intentional. According to Tim Brown of IDEO, "How" expresses optimism that solutions can be found, "Might" leaves room for experimentation and acknowledges that ideas may or may not succeed, and "We" emphasizes teamwork and collective problem solving (Hanington & Martin, 2019).
whenToUse: When you have collected user research and need to turn insights into opportunities for design.
When you want to reframe a problem as an open-ended question so teams can explore multiple possibilities instead of one predetermined solution.
When you are moving into brainstorming, because the question gives direction while still encouraging creative and diverse ideas.
When you want to encourage divergent thinking and consider different perspectives rather than one narrow approach.
When you want a common focus for discussion, so teams can collaborate and build ideas together.
howToDoIt: Identify your starting material: Name what you are working from, such as a design brief, a problem statement, or key insights from your research.
Turn the problem into HMW questions: Rewrite the problem or insight as one or more "how might we" questions, and refine them until the team agrees on the most effective version.
Generate ideas: Use the HMW question as a starting point to brainstorm a wide range of possible solutions, encouraging both individual and group creativity.
Evaluate and prioritize ideas: Review the ideas and decide which have the most potential, keeping in mind that this is an early step in an ongoing process of developing and improving solutions.
whatYouNeed: Sticky notes or a digital brainstorming tool (e.g., Miro or google docs)
Collaborative team or group for discussion
Space to organize and review ideas (physical board or digital workspace)
tips: Begin with the key problems or insights you discovered during your research, so the question is grounded in evidence.
Do not build a specific solution into the question. Keep it open-ended rather than solution-focused.
Keep the question open enough to allow a range of ideas.
Center the question on the goal or outcome you want to achieve, so it is focused but flexible.
Write the question in a positive, possibility-focused way.
Keep the user at the center of the question.
mistakes: Jumping straight to solutions.
Not grounding questions in research.
Framing the wrong problem.
Making questions too narrow.
Making questions too broad.
Ignoring user needs.
methods.example:
A hospital team notices that patients often feel confused and anxious during discharge. They turn this insight into an HMW question: "How might we make discharge instructions easier to understand?" They brainstorm ideas such as simplified guides, videos, and follow-up messages.

A college identifies that students struggle to stay organized in online classes. They frame the issue as "How might we help students manage their coursework more effectively?" and explore solutions such as better dashboard design, reminders, and planning tools.
sources: LUMA Institute. (2021, July 22). Statement starters. https://www.luma-institute.com/statement-starters/

Hanington, B., & Martin, B. (2019). Universal methods of design, expanded and revised: 125 ways to research complex problems, develop innovative ideas, and design effective solutions. Rockport Publishers.
Rosala, M. (2024, January 31). Using "how might we" questions to ideate on the right problems. Nielsen Norman Group. https://www.nngroup.com/articles/how-might-we-questions/

methods.name: Symmetric Clustering Matrix
methods.whatItIs: Every item is scored against every other item for relatedness, and the matrix is then reordered to reveal clusters. The arithmetic surfaces groupings that are difficult to perceive by eye in a large set.
methods.reference: Kumar, V. (2013). 101 design methods: A structured approach for driving innovation in your organization. Wiley. Method 4.10.
sources: Kumar, V. (2013). 101 design methods: A structured approach for driving innovation in your organization. Wiley. Method 4.10.

methods.name: Task Analysis
methods.whatItIs: A user's workflow is decomposed into its constituent actions, decisions, and system responses. The breakdown exposes redundant steps, hidden dependencies, and the points where errors are most likely.
methods.reference: Martin, B., & Hanington, B. (2012). Universal methods of design. Rockport Publishers. Method 84, p. 174.
sources: Martin, B., & Hanington, B. (2012). Universal methods of design. Rockport Publishers. Method 84, p. 174.

methods.name: Ten Types of Innovation Diagnostics
methods.whatItIs: An organization's offerings are assessed across ten distinct categories of innovation, from profit model to customer engagement. Plotting where effort is concentrated reveals the dimensions competitors have neglected.
methods.reference: Kumar, V. (2013). 101 design methods: A structured approach for driving innovation in your organization. Wiley. Method 2.9.
sources: Kumar, V. (2013). 101 design methods: A structured approach for driving innovation in your organization. Wiley. Method 2.9.

methods.name: Territory Maps
methods.imageAlt: Digital whiteboard with yellow sticky notes grouped in clusters under pink topic headings.
methods.whatItIs: Territory mapping is a visual synthesis method used to organize large amounts of qualitative research data into broader themes or "territories." It helps designers identify patterns across user experiences and uncover opportunity areas for design.
whenToUse: When you have collected a large amount of qualitative research data and need to organize it.
When exploring opportunity areas and gaps in user needs.
When you want to identify patterns and relationships across user experiences.
When defining the scope of a design problem before ideation.
howToDoIt: Gather research data: Collect notes, interview transcripts, and observations from your research.
Review and highlight insights: Identify recurring ideas, behaviors, and patterns.
Break insights into notes: Write each observation as a short, clear statement.
Group related ideas: Cluster similar notes based on shared themes.
Define territories: Combine clusters into broader categories representing key experience areas.
Label clearly: Use simple and descriptive names for each territory.
Create the visual map: Arrange territories in a structured layout to show relationships.
Refine collaboratively: Review with your team and adjust for clarity and accuracy.
whatYouNeed: Sticky notes or digital tools (Miro, FigJam)
tips: Keep territories broad but meaningful.
Use simple and clear labels.
Stay open to unexpected patterns.
Focus on trends rather than individual data points.
Work with others to reduce bias.
mistakes: Creating too many small or overly detailed categories.
Forcing data into categories that don't fit.
Using vague or unclear labels.
Skipping synthesis and jumping to solutions.
Working alone without validation.
methods.example: A design team working on a fitness app analyzes interview data about users' workout habits and challenges. They create a territory map with categories such as motivation, routines, barriers, and social influence. This process reveals that users struggle most with consistency due to lack of accountability. The team uses this insight to design features focused on habit-building and social support.
sources: Martin, B., & Hanington, B. (2012). Universal methods of design. Rockport Publishers.
Kumar, V. (2013). 101 design methods: A structured approach for driving innovation in your organization. Wiley.

Dam, R. F., & Teo, Y. S. (2016, November 17). Affinity diagrams: How to cluster your ideas and reveal insights. Interaction Design Foundation. https://ixdf.org/literature/article/affinity-diagrams-learn-how-to-cluster-and-bundle-ideas-and-facts
LUMA Institute. (2021, March 4). LUMA book and cards. https://www.luma-institute.com/our-offerings/book-and-cards/

methods.name: Thematic Networks
methods.whatItIs: Textual data is coded into basic themes, grouped into organizing themes, and consolidated into global themes, then drawn as a web. The explicit hierarchy makes the path from raw quotation to conclusion auditable.
methods.reference: Martin, B., & Hanington, B. (2012). Universal methods of design. Rockport Publishers. Method 86, p. 178.
sources: Martin, B., & Hanington, B. (2012). Universal methods of design. Rockport Publishers. Method 86, p. 178.

methods.name: Top Five

library.book: The Field Guide to Human-Centered Design (IDEO.org, 2015)
library.title: Top Five

methods.whatItIs: A team selects and ranks the five most compelling findings, ideas, or quotes from a larger set. The hard constraint forces explicit trade-offs and produces a shareable summary that a wider audience can absorb.
methods.reference: IDEO.org. (2015). The field guide to human-centered design. IDEO.org. Page 79.
sources: IDEO.org. (2015). The field guide to human-centered design. IDEO.org. Page 79.

methods.name: Visualize the Vote
methods.whatItIs: Visualize the Vote is a quick, visual poll of collaborators. Each person places a limited number of voting tokens, usually sticky notes or dots, on the ideas they favor, so the group can see preferences at a glance and discuss them.
whenToUse: When gathering group input in workshops or brainstorming sessions.
When you need to quickly reach consensus in a diverse group with differing opinions.
When narrowing down research findings into actionable focus areas.
howToDoIt: Name the subject: Tell participants what the poll is about.
Hand out tokens: Give each reviewer sticky notes or dots to use as votes.
Assign votes: Give each person one token for an overall vote and two more tokens for detail votes.
Explain the criteria: State clearly what people should vote for.
Present the ideas: Have each presenter describe a concept, then ask everyone to vote at the same time so no one is influenced by others.
Count the votes: Tally the tokens on each concept.
Discuss: Invite people to explain what they voted for and why.
tips: Keep instructions simple and time-bound.
Encourage participants to spread their votes strategically.
Use a different color for the detail votes, or for each topic when voting on several topics.
Make sure every idea is clearly visible and easy to understand before voting begins.
Start a discussion after voting so people share the reasoning behind their choices.
mistakes: Not clearly explaining voting criteria beforehand.
Allowing participants to influence each other before voting.
Having too many options without grouping or organizing them first.
Skipping the discussion phase after tallying votes.
Letting dominant voices override quieter participants' input.
methods.example: A videogame company is brainstorming a new game and uses dot voting to prioritize ideas. After presenting all concepts, each team member places their votes on the concepts they find most valuable. The team quickly identifies the top three ideas and discusses why they stood out, helping guide the next phase of development.
sources: LUMA Institute. (2012). Innovating for people: Handbook of human-centered design methods. LUMA Institute.
LUMA Institute. (n.d.). Visualize the vote. https://www.luma-institute.com
Liedtka, J., & Ogilvie, T. (2011). Designing for growth: A design thinking toolkit for managers. Columbia University Press.
Dotmocracy.org. (n.d.). How to use dot voting effectively.

methods.name: Word Clouds
methods.imageAlt: Word cloud of terms from the television series Parks and Recreation, with Pawnee, Parks, Campaign, Dream, Love, and Ann as the largest words.
methods.imageSource: Parks and Recreation, created by Greg Daniels and Michael Schur, as stated by the student
methods.whatItIs: Word Clouds are a visual representation of text data where the size of each word indicates its frequency or importance within a given body of text. They provide an immediate, "at-a-glance" summary of the most prominent themes or terms in a dataset.
whenToUse: When you're staring at 200 survey responses and need to find the "big ideas" fast.
When you need a presentation slide that shows at a glance what your users care about.
Early in the analysis phase to see if there are any weird patterns or surprises you missed.
When you need to compare two different groups, like seeing if "Free" is a big word for Trial users but "Reliable" is the big word for Pro users.
howToDoIt: Get all your notes, survey answers, or interview quotes into one doc.
Get rid of words that do not help, like "the," "basically," or "maybe." Fix spelling mistakes so "App" and "Apps" count as the same word.
Throw it into a free online tool like a word cloud maker. Let the software do the counting and sizing.
Pick a font and layout that is not a mess. The most important words should be right in the middle so they hit you immediately.
whatYouNeed: "Stop Word" list (to filter out the boring stuff)
About 20 minutes to clean and tweak the visual
tips: Context: A giant word like "Help" doesn't tell you if the help was good or bad. Always go back to the quotes to check the tone.
Filter: If you're researching a coffee app, the word "Coffee" is going to be huge. Filter it out so you can see the interesting words underneath.
Conciseness: If there are too many words, condense and clean up the text first.
mistakes: Just because a word is big does not mean it is the whole story, it just means it is the loudest.
If you leave in "it," "and," and "but," your cloud is going to be useless.
Using the cloud as the final answer instead of using it as a reason to go back and read the actual feedback.
methods.example: We sent out a survey to 500 people asking what they thought of our library. We expected to see words like "Books" and "Quiet" all over the place. Instead, when we ran the Word Cloud, the word "Community" was massive, and "Books" was tiny. It was a total "aha!" moment. It turned out people did not just want a place to borrow stuff; they wanted a place to hang out and meet people. We stopped worrying so much about the bookshelves and started planning more events and lounge spaces because that is what the data was actually telling us.
sources: WordClouds.com. (n.d.). https://www.wordclouds.com/
Vevox. (n.d.). Word cloud explained. https://vevox.zendesk.com/hc/en-us/articles/360009930318-Word-cloud-explained

methods.name: Alternative Worlds
methods.imageAlt: Hospital patient room styled like a hotel room, with a bed, designer red chairs, a flat-screen television, and warm wood paneling.
methods.whatItIs: Alternative Worlds is a method for looking at how a problem might be solved in a different context.
whenToUse: When you have difficulty coming up with a solution or overcoming mental blocks.
When you are solving complex problems and need out-of-the-box ideas.
When you want to innovate and change your market.
howToDoIt: Define a topic: Clearly identify the issue you need to solve.
Pick your alternate worlds: Choose two or three "worlds" that differ from your own world or context.
Step into each world: Brainstorm ideas based on each world by asking how that world would react to the issue.
Apply the insights: Use the new ideas to address the issue in your own world.
whatYouNeed: 2-3 hours to ideate and apply solutions
tips: Choose a world with key differences from your own.
Do not choose your competitor.
Find someone in the alternate world to interview for insight.
Build a diverse team.
Spend time learning how your alternate world operates.
mistakes: Choosing your competitor as an alternate world.
Choosing alternate worlds that do not contrast well.
Lacking specificity, which leaves the team uninspired.
Using a team that lacks diversity.
methods.example: A coffee shop is trying to create a new method of online ordering for customers. They get a group of people together to design the interface. They give a set of alternate worlds including looking at it as video game developers, people who have never used a phone, and as visually impaired adults. They then take the ideas they come up with to create a website that is easy to traverse and accessible.
sources: Alternative Worlds | LUMA Institute. (2022, June). LUMA Institute. https://www.luma-institute.com/alternative-worlds/
Alternative Worlds. (2022). Open Practice Library. https://openpracticelibrary.com/practice/alternative-worlds/
Västrik, J. (2024, December 20). "What If?" Brainstorming Technique - Julia Västrik. Julia Västrik - Team Coaching and Training. https://juliavastrik.com/facilitation/what-if-brainstorming-technique/

methods.name: Analogous Inspiration

library.book: The Field Guide to Human-Centered Design (IDEO.org, 2015)
library.title: Analogous Inspiration

methods.whatItIs: A team studies a setting that shares an underlying pattern with their problem but comes from an unrelated field, such as a pit crew for a hospital handoff. Distance from the original domain loosens assumptions that feel like constraints.
methods.reference: IDEO.org. (2015). The field guide to human-centered design. IDEO.org. Page 53.
sources: IDEO.org. (2015). The field guide to human-centered design. IDEO.org. Page 53.

methods.name: Bodystorming
methods.imageAlt: Overhead view of people moving around a floor layout drawn in chalk, with zones labeled for kitchen stations.
methods.whatItIs: Bodystorming is a hands-on technique where participants physically act out scenarios. Participants act in a real-world situation, and the observers attempt to identify potential issues or places of improvement.
whenToUse: When you are working with something physical.
When you need to simulate a real-world situation.
When working with specific locations.
When dealing with moments with large amounts of movement.
When you are attempting to understand user emotions or context.
howToDoIt: Define the situation and context: Identify what the location is and what the circumstances are.

Gather your group: Assemble a group similar in size to the group that would deal with the environment in the real situation. Participants should have the same relative knowledge as the people who would interact with it.
Simulate the environment: Find a location and set up objects that represent parts of the environment. Make sure things are labeled and clear.
Act out scenarios: Come up with scenarios that would occur in the real environment and assign the group different tasks.
Observe and identify issues: Run the scenarios and identify problem areas or places where the setup needs adjustment.
Discuss solutions: As a group, walk through the issues you found and determine how to solve them.
whatYouNeed: Various objects to simulate the environment
tips: Make the environment as accurate to real life as you can.
Avoid giving participants too many instructions, so you can see how the environment functions without explicit details.
mistakes: Not setting up an accurate environment.
Not assigning clear roles.
Restricting creativity.
Not recording properly.
methods.example: A restaurant wants to improve its kitchen, which becomes congested during busy hours. The team goes outside and draws an area on the ground that matches the current layout of the kitchen. Workers come in and go through different scenarios. After each scenario, the team speaks with the participants and ideates points of change. They run the simulation again and repeat until the kitchen can run with no issues.
sources: Segura, E. M., Vidal, L. T., & Rostami, A. (2016). Bodystorming for movement-based interaction design. Human Technology, 12(2), 193-251. https://doi.org/10.17011/ht/urn.201611174655
Smith, B. K. (2014). Bodystorming mobile learning experiences. TechTrends, 58, 71-76. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11528-013-0723-4

methods.name: Brainstorm Graphic Organizers
methods.imageAlt: Cluster web graphic organizer with a central main topic, four subtopics, and two detail bubbles on each subtopic.
methods.whatItIs: Brainstorm graphic organizers use visual diagrams to add structure to new or existing ideas from a design team. They give team members a visual way to communicate and build on one another's ideas, and they help teams challenge assumptions and consider unconventional alternatives (Martin & Hanington, 2012).
whenToUse: When you are near the beginning of the ideation phase and ideas are still unclear.
When you need to break down complex problems in a system to identify aspects that could be refined or reworked.
When you want to help teams visualize concepts after they identify the goal of the project.
howToDoIt: Gather with the team.
Write down ideas based on achieving the desired goal.
Discuss ideas with the group. Some may overlap with one another, while others may be completely unique.
Sort and group similar ideas or concepts.
Choose the type of diagram that works best for organizing the ideas (Brainstorming Webs, Flow Charts, or Tree Diagrams).
This process can be repeated as many times as needed, as team members are able to add their ideas to new or existing groups on the chart.
whatYouNeed: Digital tools: Figma, Mural, or Canva
Physical materials: sticky notes, pens, pencils or markers, and paper
tips: Prioritize quantity over quality. The more ideas the group produces, the more useful this tool becomes.
Withhold judgment and build on each other's ideas, as in any brainstorming session.
mistakes: Shutting down other members' ideas right away. The focus should be on gathering as many ideas as possible.
methods.example: This method can be used in developing a UI for a mobile app, as designers will need to determine who their target users are, how the user will interact with the app, and reasons why users will choose this app over similar existing ones. Since these concepts can vary per user, Graphic Organizers can be an effective way to organize huge amounts of ideas for each of these concerns.
sources: Martin, B., & Hanington, B. (2012). Universal methods of design. Rockport Publishers.
Visme. (2019, September 12). 15 different types of graphic organizers for education [2021]. Visme Blog. https://visme.co/blog/graphic-organizer/
Miro. (2024). Types of graphic organizers explained. https://miro.com/graphic-organizer/types/

methods.name: Brainstorming
methods.imageAlt: A glowing lightbulb with colorful icons and doodles streaming outward from it, suggesting a flow of ideas.

library.book: The Field Guide to Human-Centered Design (IDEO.org, 2015)
library.title: Brainstorm

methods.whatItIs: Brainstorming is a way to explore many ideas around a topic. Wild ideas are welcome at first and are then refined into an effective idea that can serve as a possible solution.
whenToUse: When you are deciding which research topic to focus on.
When you are choosing a topic for a How Might We question.
When you need a spark of creativity and want to produce ideas rapidly.
When you are collaborating, because building on each other's ideas expands the collection of ideas.
When you want to explore new ideas without a concrete plan.
howToDoIt: Identify the topic you want to find a solution for.
Write down as many ideas as you can in a short amount of time, without judging them.
Organize your notes into lists, affinity diagrams, or mind maps so you can build on the ideas.
Separate the ideas that can work from the ones that cannot.
Explore further the ideas that can work.
tips: Start with a clear topic.
Focus on the range of ideas you can generate rather than their quality.
Build on ideas no matter how wild they seem.
Organize your ideas, because a messy map will not help.
Evaluate carefully which ideas could provide a solution to your topic.
mistakes: Criticizing yourself over the quality of your ideas.
Not exploring the wild ideas.
Focusing on a single idea too soon, which narrows the range of options.
Not building on other people's ideas.
Not organizing or evaluating the ideas afterward.
methods.example: Clothing designers pick a topic, such as what consumers will want to buy. They quickly generate ideas about what could be trendy, what is trendy, who the target audience is, and what people will like to see. The designers then build on each other's ideas, organize them by grouping them into categories, and evaluate them to pick the most sought-after solution.
sources: IDEO.org. (2015). The field guide to human-centered design. IDEO.org.
Kumar, V. (2013). 101 design methods: A structured approach for driving innovation in your organization. Wiley.
Varsano, J. (2023). 10-for-10. Open Practice Library. https://openpracticelibrary.com/practice/10-for-10/

methods.name: Bundle Ideas
methods.imageAlt: Hands arrange sticky notes and sketches across large sheets of paper on a table, with coffee cups nearby.

library.book: The Field Guide to Human-Centered Design (IDEO.org, 2015)
library.title: Bundle Ideas

methods.whatItIs: Bundle Ideas creates fresh, refined ideas by compiling many concepts based on patterns and similar elements. It is also known as "mix and match."
whenToUse: When you are not sure where to start. Because the method is similar to brainstorming, it can help you produce creative ideas right away.
When you have a marketing task, because the method can produce many robust concepts that rejuvenate a company or clarify what a client needs.
When cooperation produces many ideas across your team and you need to sort which make the most sense, which fit best, and which seem unrealistic.
howToDoIt: Arrange all of your existing ideas in an understandable, visible way so that you can reorganize them.
Sort the ideas into clusters based on similarities. Highlight the elements you like and the elements that may fail to be realistic.
Create new groupings based on the common themes and patterns you notice in your first clusters.
Critique and refine the clusters. This step should narrow down what will actually work to solve your problem.
Highlight commonalities and mix and match ideas again to create new concepts and solutions.
whatYouNeed: Large board or paper surface to visualize your ideas
Something to write with (pens, markers, pencils)
Sticky notes or something to take notes on
Possible other participants willing to contribute insightful ideas
tips: Start off with a large amount of ideas, even if they seem disproportionate or irrelevant. This gives you much more to work with and can help refine what's actually necessary.
Be open-minded to all ideas, but remain realistic especially if you have specific limitations (budget, accessibility, etc.).
Highlight things based on what you like about it or what might work best. This will help your actual solution be successful.
mistakes: Don't be biased with your groupings. An idea may not work the best in your scenario so do not keep it around just because it may be creative or cost-efficient.
Be sure that you are grouping your ideas and not blindly brainstorming. Don't forget the main purpose behind Bundle Ideas (specifically what separates it from just being brainstorming).
Don't overcomplicate your groupings. Sometimes when trying to connect things that simply don't connect, you risk causing conflict down the line for yourself.
methods.example: You and your team want to design an app for wellness & fitness but aren't entirely sure where to start considering the many different lifestyles people live. Thus, you start with the ideation phase and begin to create a surplus of ideas that could work. After creating ideas and concepts, you and your team work together to group these ideas based on their similarities. By sifting through their common elements and highlighting possible patterns, you're able to narrow down possible solutions. You then use your remaining cluster of ideas to create a successful app that works on wellness & fitness.

methods.name: Co-Creation Session
methods.imageAlt: Overhead view of several people working around a table, placing orange sticky notes on a printed interface layout.

library.book: The Field Guide to Human-Centered Design (IDEO.org, 2015)
library.title: Co-Creation Session

methods.whatItIs: A co-creation session is an activity in which a design team invites users to participate and collaborate in designing a product.
whenToUse: When you want to create a product for a specific demographic of users.
When you are designing a landscape that will affect a neighborhood.
When you want new ideas and perspectives from people outside the design team.
howToDoIt: Prepare: Define what you are designing for, who your target audience is, how you will reach your users, and what your goals are.
Prepare the activity: Create a toolkit for users. Decide which materials they will design with, where the session will take place, and how much collaboration you want.
Run the workshop: Engage with participants, document what they make, and ask them about their designs and their experiences with them.
Turn designs into prototypes: Take the users' ideas and start sketching and building them.
Finalize the product: Make final versions of the products and compare them with the designs the users came up with.
whatYouNeed: Consent from a variety of users to be documented, interviewed, and to participate
A dedicated workspace where designers and users can work together
A variety of supplies users can use to develop their designs, such as paper, markers, glue, and scissors
Ways to document: a camera, video recorder, or audio recorder
Ways to take notes: a notepad, sketchpad, pens, or a laptop
tips: Know which topic you want to focus on.
Encourage users to come up with as many designs as possible. Nothing is off the table.
Make it clear that you are interested in what they have to say.
Make sure the users communicate with each other.
Ask users to elaborate on their designs and explain why they like them.
mistakes: Letting the session stop being collaborative, or letting conflicts of interest shape the results.
Not having enough time and supplies.
Letting personal biases shape the session.
Losing track of your goal.
Judging ideas.
methods.example: You want to design a park that will be next to a neighborhood that is in an impoverished area, and you want to hear the opinions of the people who live in the neighborhood. You set up a co-creation session where the user collaborates on the design of the park and what features are part of the new park. You document their ideas and wants and make sure to incorporate them in the final design.

methods.name: Concept Metaphors and Analogies
methods.imageAlt: People sit around a low table covered with large sheets of paper, sketching and writing with colored pencils.
methods.whatItIs: This method generates ideas by comparing your problem or concept to something familiar. A metaphor is a vivid, nonliteral comparison (a mobile phone is a wallet), while an analogy compares more directly (budgeting is like managing weight loss). Both reframe conventional thinking (Kumar, 2013).
whenToUse: When you are stuck or out of ideas.
When you want more creative thinking.
When a concept feels too complicated.
During brainstorming.
howToDoIt: Define your problem.
List key traits (confusing, fast, stressful, etc.).
Compare it to something similar (like a maze, game, or journey).
Turn that comparison into ideas.
Push it further and don't stop at one idea.
Sketch or describe your ideas.
Pick what works best.
tips: Do not overthink. Go for unexpected comparisons.
Use multiple metaphors, not just one.
Push ideas beyond the obvious.
Prompt comparisons with questions such as "acts like," "looks like," or "works like" (Kumar, 2013).
mistakes: Choosing metaphors that are too literal.
Not translating the metaphor into actual design ideas.
Stopping at the first idea.
Playing it safe instead of exploring.
methods.example: A team designing a mental health app reframes it as a "garden." This leads to features like "planting habits," "tracking growth," and "removing weeds," creating a softer and more engaging user experience.
sources: Casakin, H. (2007). Metaphors in design problem solving. International Journal of Design. https://www.ijdesign.org/index.php/IJDesign/article/view/53/27
Interaction Design Foundation. (2022). Learn how to use analogies. https://ixdf.org/literature/article/learn-how-to-use-the-best-ideation-methods-analogies

methods.name: Concept-Generating Matrix
methods.whatItIs: Two sets of categories form the axes of a grid, and ideas are generated in each intersecting cell. Requiring an idea in every cell produces combinations a team would not reach through open discussion.
methods.reference: Kumar, V. (2013). 101 design methods: A structured approach for driving innovation in your organization. Wiley. Method 5.6.

methods.name: Creative Toolkits
methods.imageAlt: Flat lay of creative toolkit supplies on a wooden table, including markers, colored pencils, scissors, tape, sticky notes, construction paper, a ruler, and a notebook.
methods.imageSource: the Creative Toolkits group project by Gloria Eban, 2026
methods.whatItIs: Creative toolkits are collections of materials that let participants build or draw a solution of their own. Watching what people make with the supplies shows designers what they naturally look for in a solution.
whenToUse: When you are in the research phase and want to learn the aspirations and dreams of users.
When you want to uncover concerns and subconscious feelings that surface through the process of creating.
When you want to learn how participants feel from the way they create, not only from what they create.
When you want to discover what park users look for in a space, such as the features, colors, and aesthetic that attract them to a recreational area.
When you want to understand the emotions participants feel about needs in a particular situation, such as school.
When you want to spark creativity that designers can use in creating a product, such as a new toy for elementary-aged children.
howToDoIt: Define: Decide on the specific problem you want to understand from the users' perspective. Write a prompt that gives participants the scope of the problem and an outline for a possible solution.
Gather materials: Prepare a 2D or 3D toolkit that fits your research question, problem, or prompt.
Gather participants: Recruit users who relate to the research problem and could reveal emotions and needs about it.
Prepare participants: Explain the process, the prompt, the supplies, and the instructions.
Sensitize: Provide materials that bring out participants' emotions and feelings about the subject, problem, or activity.

Create and observe: Set a time limit if needed and have participants create something in response to the prompt. It could be a collage or a 3D model, abstract or simple. While they work, observe how they choose materials, how they use the limited supplies, and why they make what they make.
Learn: From your observations and the final product, identify the need or emotion each participant was trying to communicate.
whatYouNeed: Supplies that depend on the research problem or prompt
2D supplies: colored or white paper, magazine cutouts, markers, pencils, pens, crayons, glue, tape, scissors, and stickers
3D supplies: clay, paint, wire, pipe cleaners, paper, glue, tape, cardboard, felt, toy building blocks, and Velcro
tips: Give participants enough information to know where to start.
Offer a variety of supplies, even unconventional ones, to spark creativity.
Keep the kit organized and portable so it can be reused across sessions and locations.
mistakes: Interfering while the activity is in session, which biases the results.
Over-explaining or steering participants toward a particular final product, which hides their authentic needs and feelings.
Treating the toolkit as the goal. Its purpose is to help people express what is hard to say in words.
methods.example: Designers for the county schools may want to know what students look for on a school playground. In a group of students, primarily elementary aged, designers would have students sit down with a provided assortment of materials, such as clay, paper, tape, glue, paint, markers, crayons, pens, and Legos. With these materials, students can build or draw what they look for in a playground that they will visit for recess everyday. The process will reveal to designers the imagination that students have and how they would plan on using a playground to fulfill that imagination.
sources: Design Kit. (n.d.). Collage. https://www.designkit.org/methods/collage.html
Hanington, B., & Martin, B. (2012). Universal methods of design. Rockport Publishers.

methods.name: Design Charette
methods.whatItIs: Designers and stakeholders work together in a short, intensive session to produce and critique many ideas quickly. The compressed timeframe and mixed participation surface disagreement early, while it is still inexpensive to resolve.
methods.reference: Martin, B., & Hanington, B. (2012). Universal methods of design. Rockport Publishers. Method 26, p. 58.

methods.name: Design Workshops
methods.imageAlt: Workshop participants stand at a wall covered in sticky notes beneath the heading What does success look like?
methods.whatItIs: A design workshop is a session in which collaborators come together to solve problems within a design project. Workshops are a form of participatory design that organizes creative co-design methods into sessions where several participants work alongside members of the design team (Martin & Hanington, 2012).
whenToUse: When a design project has just started and you are gathering information, involving stakeholders, and learning users' needs.
When you are gathering ideas by sketching plans, finding solutions, and exploring different ways to approach the design process.
When you are testing and prototyping and need feedback on the project.
When you need to compare ideas and see which ones work best.
When you need to secure buy-in from team members and clients.
howToDoIt: Define the goal of the workshop.
Gather your team of designers and invite the participants. Balance the number of facilitators with the number of participants, and give everyone a clear role.
Plan the agenda and timing, and collect the materials the activities need.

Open the session with an overview and the agenda. Run the activities, such as group discussion of concerns, ideas on sticky notes organized into affinity diagrams, mind maps, collages, drawings, and brainstorming.
Document the session as it happens and collect the work outcomes afterward.
Organize and test the ideas, then follow up with each participant after the workshop.
tips: Make a plan, which helps with organization and makes ideas easier to process.
Set a goal that the session can meet.
Create a welcoming environment that is not stressful or chaotic.
Encourage every participant to do their best and support them.
Stay on plan, but remain ready to adapt to changing circumstances and the needs of the team.
End the session with steps that lead toward a solution.
mistakes: Creating an agenda that is too big.
Not having a clear goal.
Letting one person control everything instead of everyone working together.
Skipping the prep work.
Not gathering ideas.
Not following up with each participant after the workshop.
methods.example: NC State University wants to improve its dorms. A workshop invites students who lived in the freshman dorms to respond to prompts such as: What issues occurred while you stayed in the dorms, and how could they be improved for better living? In what ways did the dorm make you feel at home, and when did it make you feel unwelcome? Participants write their answers on sticky notes, and the group clusters them to identify priorities.

methods.name: Draw It
methods.imageAlt: Hand-drawn community map on paper with handwritten labels, small icons, red and green hearts, and arrows showing places and routes.
methods.imageNote: Cropped to show only the hand-drawn map.

library.book: The Field Guide to Human-Centered Design (IDEO.org, 2015)
library.title: Draw It

methods.whatItIs: Using sketching and drawing instead of words to unlock new visual solutions during team ideation.
whenToUse: When you want to understand experiences, routines, or systems that are easier to explain visually than verbally.
When you are in early research and ideation, at the start of a project, and want to understand people's behaviors, habits, and everyday experiences before developing solutions.
When language or communication barriers exist, because participants may be more comfortable showing an experience than explaining it in words.

When participants struggle to describe a complex or hard-to-explain experience through conversation alone. Drawing can help organize their thoughts and reveal relationships, priorities, or pain points.
howToDoIt: Prepare simple materials: Have paper, a notebook, and pens ready.
Set a clear prompt: Ask the participant to draw something specific, such as a daily route, weekly spending habits, or a timeline of past jobs.
Keep the task low-pressure: Explain that it does not need to be artistic or polished.
Allow them time to draw: Give space for them to think while sketching.
Use the drawing as a conversation starter: Ask follow-up questions about what they included, what stands out, and why.
Document the drawing: Keep notes or a copy of the sketch for later analysis.
tips: Keep prompts focused and easy to understand.
Use drawing to support conversation, not replace it.
If participants feel nervous, sketch first yourself to make the activity feel more comfortable.
Ask open-ended follow-up questions such as "Can you tell me about this part?" or "Why did you place that here?".
Simple visuals like maps, timelines, and quick diagrams often work better than asking for detailed drawings.
mistakes: Focusing too much on artistic quality. The goal is insight, not a polished drawing.
Interrupting while they draw. Let them think and organize ideas first.
Treating the drawing as the final answer. The most useful insights often come from the discussion afterward.
Leading the participant. Avoid suggesting what they should include.
methods.example: While researching what happens to farmers' harvests on the way to market in a foreign country, a researcher cannot get a clear answer from a farmer, even after rephrasing the question several times. The researcher hands the farmer a sticky note with a circle and asks how many tomatoes out of the total make it to market. The farmer colors in about half of the circle, showing that half of the harvest reaches the market.

methods.name: Ideation Game
methods.imageAlt: Three smiling colleagues stand in front of a wall covered with yellow sticky notes.
methods.whatItIs: Ideation Games are basically a "hack" for people's brains. Instead of staring at a blank whiteboard and forcing "innovation," users take game mechanics, like timers, constraints, or role-playing, to make the process feel more like a low-stakes activity. It is about lowering the pressure so the weird, creative ideas naturally come out.
whenToUse: When your team is stuck in a "rut" and keeps suggesting the same basic boring ideas.
When people are too judgmental about their own ideas and will not speak up.
When you need to generate a massive quantity of ideas (Quantity > Quality) in a short amount of time.
When you need to break the ice at the start of a design project.
howToDoIt: Pick your game: Choose a format that fits your vibe. Popular ones include Crazy Eights (sketching 8 ideas in 8 minutes) or The Worst Possible Idea (aiming for the absolute worst solution).
Set the Rules: Every effective game needs some boundaries. Set a timer and a no-judgment rule.
Provide the Prompt: Give everyone a clear, "How Might We." question to solve. If it is too broad, the game will stall; if it's too narrow, the ideas will be boring.
Play the Round: Let people go wild. If it is a drawing game, tell them stick figures are fine. If it is a word game, tell them typos don't matter.
Reflect and Sort: Once the game is over, look at the pile of chaos you created. Pick out the ideas that actually have a spark and move those into your serious design phase.
tips: If an idea feels too "stupid," that is usually a sign it is pushing a boundary. Do not delete it.
Playing upbeat, wordless music in the background can keep the energy high and prevent awkward silences.
mistakes: Taking it too seriously.
Running too long.
No follow-up discussion.
methods.example: Our team was trying to redesign a student portal, but every idea we had felt like something from 2005. We were bored, and the energy in the room was dead. We decided to play "The Anti-Problem" instead of asking "How do we make this easy to use?", we asked "How could we make this the most frustrating experience ever?" Suddenly, people were shouting out hilarious, terrible ideas: "Make the login button move every time you try to click it!" or "Require a 50-character password that changes every hour!" By looking at those "bad" ideas, we realized the core of the frustration was actually navigation. We flipped the "moving button" idea into a "persistent navigation bar" that solved the real issue. The game broke the tension and got us to the finish line.
sources: SessionLab. (n.d.). Brainstorming techniques. https://www.sessionlab.com/blog/brainstorming-techniques/
Gamestorming. (n.d.). Games for fresh thinking and ideas. https://gamestorming.com/category/games-for-fresh-thinking-and-ideas/

methods.name: Image Boards
methods.imageAlt: Black board covered with cut-out vintage photographs of women, clothing, a telephone, and office scenes, arranged as a mood board.
methods.imageSource: Alexander Huls, Setting the Mood: How to Create Great Mood Boards for Your Project
methods.whatItIs: An image board, also called a mood board, brings together images, patterns, and text to create a certain emotion or feeling at first glance. It communicates aesthetics, style, audience, or context (Martin & Hanington, 2012).
whenToUse: In the early stages of a design process, likely in the Define or Ideate phase, once the team has decided on a general focus for aesthetics, style, context, or audience.
When you are designing a brand logo and want to show how different color schemes may look to others.
Before buying furniture for an empty space, to show the colors, textures, and furniture that might appear in it.
When you are creating a website for a business and want to show interfaces and images before agreeing on a look.
howToDoIt: Review existing materials: Look at the style guides and forms of identity already established for the company or business, and use them as a starting point.
Select the tool: Choose a physical or digital tool or layout.

Choose the moods: Think about the product in relation to its users, including the mood and emotion that come from the product and how you want users to feel when interacting with it. Write down words and group them.
Collect the visuals: Find images that relate to the theme.
Arrange the visuals: Arrange the images you collected, sorting them by importance and by how well they deliver the mood.
Share the board: Share the board with others to gain feedback and different perspectives. If teammates made different boards, compare them and see what is similar.
tips: Create several mood boards as experiments to find the best one.
Hold a mood board workshop with other people to help generate ideas.
When choosing words for the moods, pick four or five that best capture the general theme.
Use white space on the board to create separation.
Color code the feedback in the last step.
Consider the kind of board you need: a style board, a user-based board that profiles the audience, or an environment-based board that shows the surroundings for the design.
mistakes: Using too many images, which can steer specific ideas into the final outcome.
Building physical boards without planning for the time and waste of printing and materials.
Mixing contradicting images, which makes the board messy.
methods.example: A graphic designer meets with a new client that intends to launch a coffee brand but has trouble explaining the look that they want. The designer creates a mood board filled with different earthy color palettes, different styles, and cozy cafe images to help with the visualization of the brand. When they meet again, the client points out the different elements he can connect with the most, which helps decide on a clear direction on the design. The mood board was a big help in saving time and preventing miscommunication before the design process.
sources: Yang, L. (2023, February 26). Mood boards in UX: How and why to use them. Nielsen Norman Group. https://www.nngroup.com/articles/mood-boards/

Huls, A. (2019, June 11). Setting the mood: How to create great mood boards for your project. Pond5 Blog. https://blog.pond5.com/23909-setting-the-mood-how-to-create-great-mood-boards-for-your-project/

methods.name: Mash-Ups
methods.imageAlt: Five colleagues in a bright office sit around a table with laptops while one woman stands beside a corkboard covered in sticky notes.

library.book: The Field Guide to Human-Centered Design (IDEO.org, 2015)
library.title: Mash-Ups

methods.whatItIs: Mash-ups ask you to pick a quality you want to improve in your design, such as speed, efficiency, or aesthetics. You then layer a brand that delivers that quality over your design challenge, which produces bold, even unreasonable, questions that accelerate creative thinking.
whenToUse: When you struggle with a certain quality in your design challenge.
When you are having trouble brainstorming ideas.
When you want to compare your ideas to a drastically different reference point.
When you are early in the ideation phase.
When your current solution feels too generic.
howToDoIt: Identify: Analyze a quality you want in your solution, such as efficiency, speed, aesthetics, or accuracy, and find brands or services that deliver it successfully.
Layer: Layer the brand over your design challenge and form a mash-up question, for example, "What is a streaming service version of a classroom?"
Brainstorm: Use the question to brainstorm combinations that would work in your project context, and capture all of your ideas on sticky notes.
Collaborate: Return to your group and discuss the prompts you came up with.
Narrow: Start narrowing down ideas from your group's prompts. Do not worry too much about this last step, because the process is about producing as many ideas as possible.
tips: Start with the most outlandish ideas, then come up with more realistic solutions.
Choose a reference brand that differs strongly from your design challenge.
mistakes: Choosing a design challenge and reference brand that are too similar, which makes it harder to produce creative ideas.
Not branching out of your comfort zone.
Limiting your ideas because they are not realistic.
methods.example: Your library wants to improve how engaging its experience is to attract a broader demographic (the quality). For reference, you look at Disney World theme parks, because they attract many demographics. You come up with the mash-up question, "What is Disney World's version of a library?" and arrive at placing miniature mascots around the library to make it more inviting for all ages.
sources: IDEO.org. (2015). The field guide to human-centered design. https://www.designkit.org/resources/1.html
IDEO U. (2026). Ideation method: Mash-up. https://www.ideou.com/pages/ideation-method-mash-up

methods.name: Morphological Synthesis
methods.imageAlt: Matrix with four columns labeled Variable 1 through Variable 4, each holding sticky notes marked Idea, with a line linking one chosen idea in each column.
methods.whatItIs: Morphological synthesis is a structured ideation method that comes from engineering. It generates solutions by decomposing a problem into key components, listing the possible variations for each, and recombining them. Concepts are organized under user-centered categories, such as activities, user needs, product functions, or design principles, and complementary concepts from each category are combined into solutions. A solution is a set of concepts that work together as a complete system (Kumar, 2013).
whenToUse: When you want to generate new concepts, or to organize concepts you already have under user-centered categories.
When you need to combine complementary concepts into complete solutions instead of isolated ideas.
When you are in the idea generation phase and want a structured alternative to free brainstorming.
When you are working in fields such as engineering design, policy analysis, product design, or scenario development, or looking for new product or patent ideas.
howToDoIt: Select categories: Choose the user-centered categories that organize your concepts, such as user needs, user activities, product functions, or design principles. These are the key attributes that play a role in your challenge.
Build the morphological chart: Write the categories next to each other in the first row, then list the related concepts beneath each one to form columns.

Combine complementary concepts: Select a concept from each column and combine it with complementary concepts from the other columns. Write a brief description of how each combined solution works as a system.
Compare and evaluate: Rank the solutions by how well they meet your user-centered criteria.
Document and refine: Record the solutions, discuss how to evaluate them further, and refine them into complete solutions.
whatYouNeed: A morphological chart (matrix) or sticky notes
A list of categories or attributes
A set of concepts, either existing or newly generated
Criteria for evaluating the combined solutions
A team to combine and evaluate concepts (optional)
tips: Treat the method as evolutionary. You can refine the categories as you go.
Use sticky notes if you want a hands-on, movable way to try combinations instead of a fixed matrix.
Choose categories from the user's point of view, such as activities and needs, so the solutions stay user-centered.
mistakes: Expecting free-form creativity from a method that is highly structured.
Generating more combinations than you can evaluate. Set evaluation criteria in advance.
Combining concepts at random without checking that they work together as a system.
methods.example:
A production agency wants to create a new TV format. The team chooses three attributes for the top of its matrix: target audience, type of show, and theme. It lists ten components for each, such as children, elderly, and teens for audience; game show, quiz, and reality TV for type; and history, humor, and sports for theme. Combining children, quiz, and politics suggests a quiz program that makes kids more interested in politics, hosted by a young, energetic children's idol who asks two teams of clever kids questions about politics (de Ruijter, 2023).

In a student project on urban dating, a team identified four main activities as its categories: preparing, finding, connecting, and follow-up. It combined complementary concepts from each column into holistic solutions, such as a system that joins Flirting Coach, Matchmaker, Dinner for Eight, and Relationship Warranty for shy and cautious daters (Kumar, 2013).
sources: Daly Research Group. (n.d.). Comparing ideation techniques for beginning designers. University of Michigan. https://dalyresearch.engin.umich.edu/wp-content/uploads/sites/237/2018/02/Comparing-ideation-techniques-for-beginning-designers.pdf
