methods.name: Round Robin
methods.imageAlt: Round Robin brainstorming board with six rows of colored sticky notes, one row per round, and a list of six team members, each assigned a color.
methods.whatItIs: Round Robin is an iterative brainstorming technique where a single idea is passed from person to person in a group, allowing each member to contribute to and build upon the previous person's work.
whenToUse: When you need to generate a high volume of diverse ideas quickly.
When trying to overcome groupthink or any dominant voices in a meeting.
When a core concept exists but needs multi-disciplinary refinement.
When the team is stuck and needs a structured way to evolve an existing thought.
howToDoIt: Define the problem statement or core idea clearly to the entire group.
Distribute templates or sheets to each participant and have them write down one initial idea.
Pass the sheet to the person on the right after a set time limit, like 2 to 3 minutes.
Iterate by having the next person add a feature, solve a flaw, or expand the idea they just received in some way.
Repeat the passing process until the sheet has circled the entire group.
Review the completed sheets and cluster the most promising evolved ideas.
tips: Welcome any idea rather than critiquing during the passing phase.
Keep the time intervals short to maintain high energy and prevent overthinking.
mistakes: Evaluating or criticizing ideas before the round is finished.
Passing the paper too early or too late, which can break the group's rhythm.
methods.example: A design team was tasked with improving the city's public transit app. During a Round Robin session, one member suggested "live bus tracking," and sent that paper to the person on their right. The next person then added "crowd density alerts," and the next third person added "an incentive or reward for off-peak travel." This collaborative layering resulted in a comprehensive feature set that no single designer had envisioned alone.
sources: Buley, L. (2013). The User Experience Team of One: A Research and Design Survival Guide. Rosenfeld Media.
Kumar, V. (2013). 101 Design Methods: A Structured Approach for Driving Innovation in Your Organization. John Wiley & Sons.
LUMA Institute. (2012). Innovating for People: Handbook of Human-Centered Design Methods. LUMA Institute.

methods.name: Thumbnail Sketching
methods.imageAlt: Pencil thumbnail sketches in six panels showing a person who uses a wheelchair moving through a cafe, with speech bubbles and notes.
methods.whatItIs: Thumbnail sketching is a rapid way of brainstorming in which designers make small, simple sketches to explore different concepts or layouts without working out the small details. Because the sketches are small, gestural, and general, the process pushes you to explore many ideas instead of perfecting one, and it leaves room for later refinement (LUMA Institute, 2012).
whenToUse: In the early concept development phase, when ideas need to be explored quickly before committing to a direction.
When you are arranging elements in a design, poster, or illustration.
When you want to compare and discuss ideas with peers and gather feedback from clients.
When you want to get ideas out of your head and onto paper quickly.
howToDoIt: Define the problem: Identify the topic and the goal you want to explore.
Set up the page: Divide a page into small boxes, one for each idea, and gather basic drawing materials. In a team, ask each person to work independently.
Sketch quickly: Draw quick, simple ideas in the boxes, showing various possibilities. Think about one aspect of the topic at a time.
Generate variations: Change the layout, composition, or scale, and consider another aspect of the topic.
Review and compare: Look over the sketches, alone or as a group, and discuss them.
Select: Choose the strongest thumbnails based on functionality and creativity.
Refine: Develop the chosen concept with additional, more detailed sketching.
whatYouNeed: A pencil or other writing utensil
tips: Go into the method with a general approach, and refine the details as you work through it.
Color wash boxes to create contrast or to code them.
Group similar thumbnails from a project in batches to spot cross-inspirations and similarities.
Encourage visual thinking, not perfect drawings, and limit the time for each round of sketching.
mistakes: Spending time on details that do not matter, such as what faces look like, clothing, coloring, or gender, unless they have significance, such as which demographic does what in the sketches.
Not making enough sketch boxes, which limits how deeply you can expand on the concept.
Editing or judging sketches too early.
methods.example: A retail company is designing a new grocery store layout and creates several thumbnails to test aisle arrangements, product displays, and checkout placement. The team imagines how shoppers would move through the space and analyzes the flow of the store: Does it get congested in certain spaces? Is it accessible enough?

methods.name: A/B Testing
methods.imageAlt: A/B test design showing the same web page twice, with the original button design above and a test variant with a changed button below.
methods.whatItIs: A/B Testing is a quantitative research method used to compare two or more versions of a design to determine which will work better with your intended outcome. It collects information regarding what designs work better than others and by what degree, but will not explain why it works better.
whenToUse: When you need to test potential improvements in your prototype or an existing design.
When you have methods that show the pros and cons of each design, but not the efficiency in practice.
Throughout the prototyping phase to compare current designs with versions of the design that have small improvements.
When you need a simple way to communicate the advantages of a new design without technical details.
howToDoIt: Theorize impactful changes. Getting an idea of what changes will have a greater effect on your users will increase the chance that the new design is more efficient than the original. Previous research can be used to create a hypothesis on what changes will help to improve your design.

Define your improvement. Identify the aspect of your design you will improve, limiting the new design to one differing element. Create the change in designs so that it is clear what part of the design is being improved upon.

Define your goal. Determining a quantitative goal is important to identify the more efficient design. Tracking other related aspects of the design that may be affected will help to ensure you know the goal will bring a positive impact to the overall design.

Split your sample groups so that the users in each group are similar overall. This prevents any significant change in testing that would be caused by having too many differences between the users of each group.

Define a timeframe for the test to happen. The test cannot be indefinite and has to be conducted long enough for significant data to be collected. When testing designs already being used, such as a website, allow the new design to be tested for two weeks to get enough user interaction.

Analyze the results and determine which design is more efficient. If the results are inconclusive or the original design was more efficient then the original design is kept. If the new design was more efficient then it is kept to be improved upon in future iterations.
whatYouNeed: Sample group that can be split into two groups
Defined test schedule relevant to your design/prototype
tips: Testing identical designs should give inconclusive results, otherwise you can investigate the cause to decrease the chance of mistakes in regular testing.
Repeating the process often helps to supplement other methods as you understand why the changes are more efficient.
Changing as few elements as possible helps to determine why your improvements work and prevents the need of extensive changes to the overall design.
mistakes: Not having clearly defined goals will cause confusion on the purpose of the test and what the desired outcome of the design is.
Stopping testing before you have received meaningful data will lead to changes being made pre-emptively without reliable results to back the new design.
Focusing too much on one aspect of the design that is affected by the new element could cause other aspects to be impacted negatively.

Ignoring qualitative research in favor of A/B Testing can lead to false positives or negatives being implemented to the design. Making changes without understanding why they are working may cause issues in later iterations.
methods.example: In 2010, eBay wanted to test if having more listings on the webpage by making images smaller would increase user engagement. They created an A/B test by showing some users smaller images on listings and others large images while scrolling through the website. Previous testing led them to observe that showing more listings on the page would result in increased engagement and used that hypothesis for the A/B testing. Upon comparing the two designs, they found results that demonstrated high engagement when there were larger images, even though there were fewer listings that could fit on screen at one time. This led to the website showing larger images for all users across the site.
sources: Martin, B., & Hanington, B. (2019). Universal methods of design (Expanded, and Revised). Quarto Publishing Group USA.
Neusesser, T. (2024). A/B Testing 101. Nielsen Norman Group. https://www.nngroup.com/articles/ab-testing/

methods.name: Appearance Modeling
methods.imageAlt: Appearance modeling template with swatch rows for emotional qualities, visual attributes, physical characteristics, tone of voice, and color palette, plus three empty image frames.
methods.whatItIs: Appearance modeling creates a pre-production prototype that renders the design the way it should look, but has little to no functionality.
whenToUse: When you are developing software, physical products, or service offerings.
When you are designing a mobile app and want a mockup that looks fully functional, with animations and layouts, before coding begins.
When you are creating a dashboard for a new automobile, where the model shows screen placement and materials and a user can sit inside and give feedback on how it feels.
When a new restaurant is prototyping menus, uniforms, and table settings, so the model gives a full experience before the restaurant opens.
howToDoIt: Identify an idea or concept to develop.
Assemble a small team.
Decide the goals that the model will provide as information.
Consider a range of emotional qualities for the model.
Assemble a palette of colors as well as materials.
Develop different sketches to show many possibilities to the model.
Home in on a few treatments to refine.
Draw realistic renderings.
Produce models to show the finished effect of the design.
tips: 3D printing is a strong use in terms of feasibility.
Use a scaled down model to show the design.
If the model was created on a digital interface, look at it on a digital device.
mistakes: Focusing on looks instead of gaining feedback, where the designer tends to focus on making it nearly finished instead of gathering opinions.
Making the model functional too early, where money and time may be wasted before even knowing if the design is right.
Not testing all of the versions made, where a designer may stick to one design.
methods.example: A startup that is in the process of a new skincare brand uses the appearance modeling method to design multiple realistic versions of the packaging that will hold the upcoming products before production. The team at hand creates different mockups including different labels, colors, and textures to identify the best version customers will agree with. During a group session, participants compare each made mockup and provide feedback into which one they would buy. The company then chooses the best option and moves on to production.
sources: Appearance modeling. LUMA Institute. (2021a, July 22). https://www.luma-institute.com/appearance-modeling/
Advanced prototypes models. Versadyne LLC. (2025, October 17). https://versadyne.net/rapid-prototyping-services/advanced-models/
Appearance modeling template. Mural. (n.d.). https://www.mural.co/templates/appearance-modeling

methods.name: Behavioral Prototype
methods.whatItIs: A behavioral prototype is a method used in the Explore Concepts mode (before physical prototypes are made) in which, based on early concepts, teams plan a situation with simulated artifacts, environments, information, or processes and involve users in it.
whenToUse: When you are testing user interactions that rely on complex or new technology.
During early design phases, when the product concept exists but is not implemented.
When you want to evaluate the usability and intuitiveness of actions or tasks.
When you are exploring specific behavioral assumptions or design questions.
When resource, time, or technology constraints prevent you from building a real prototype.
howToDoIt: Identify the situation to be simulated: Choose a specific scenario where understanding user behavior will help improve your idea. Decide what behaviors you want to observe, and plan the simulation by including key elements like people (participants/actors), objects (artifacts), and props.
Prepare the environment: Set up a space whether physical or virtual where participants can naturally interact with the situation. Make sure it allows them to behave freely and realistically.

Engage users in the simulated situation: Invite participants and decide whether they will take part individually or in groups. Guide them through the activity so they can interact with the environment and your concept.

Observe, document, and ask questions: watch what participants do during the simulation, focusing on their actions, thoughts, and reactions. Record behaviors (video or notes) without interrupting, then ask follow-up questions afterward to understand their decisions and feelings.
Analyze and iterate: Review your observations to identify patterns in behavior. Use these insights to improve your concept, then repeat the process to refine it further.
whatYouNeed: Prototype materials (sketches, mockups, or simple models of the intervention)
Design tools (paper, digital design software, or prototyping tools)
Research data/insights about user behavior (from interviews or observations)
Test environments (real-world or simulated context where behavior occurs)
Feedback collection methods (notes, recordings, surveys, or observations)
Iteration resources (time and ability to refine and retest prototypes)
tips: Start simple and low-fidelity.
Focus on behavior, not just the interface.
Test in realistic context.
Use "Wizard of Oz" techniques when needed.
Define a clear behavioral question.
Observe, don't just ask.
mistakes: Focusing too much on visuals instead of behavior.
Overbuilding the prototype too early.
Not testing in a realistic context.
Failing to define a clear behavioral question.
Relying only on what users say.
Not using simulation techniques when needed.
methods.example:
A team designing a public transit app wants to test whether users will tap a new "Plan Trip" button placed at the top of the screen. Instead of building the full app, they create a simple clickable prototype and manually simulate results when users interact with it. By observing users in a realistic setting, such as asking them to plan a trip, the team sees whether the button naturally guides behavior or gets ignored.

A grocery store wants to encourage healthier food choices, so it tests placing signs and prompts near fresh produce. Employees act as part of the prototype by guiding or observing shoppers' decisions without changing the store layout permanently. By watching what customers actually pick up and purchase, the store learns whether the intervention influences behavior before scaling it.
sources: Kumar, V. (2013). 101 design methods: A structured approach for driving innovation in your organization. Wiley.

Tefera, Y. (2018). Behavioral prototyping: How can we test complex behavior of a product without really implementing it. methods.name: Business Model Canvas
methods.imageAlt: Business Model Canvas template with nine boxes: key partners, key activities, key resources, value propositions, customer relationships, channels, customer segments, cost structure, and revenue streams.

library.book: The Field Guide to Human-Centered Design (IDEO.org, 2015)
library.title: Business Model Canvas

methods.whatItIs: The Business Model Canvas is a one-page worksheet that helps a team think through the key parts of a business, service, or social enterprise. Its nine blocks are customer segments, value propositions, channels, customer relationships, revenue streams, key resources, key activities, key partnerships, and cost structure. Filling it out shows where the model is strong and where it has gaps.
whenToUse: When you are starting a business, service, or product and need to strategize.
When you have solidified an idea and begin to test it, and you need to keep the business model in mind.
When the business environment changes and you need to rethink your strategy.
Repeatedly as the project progresses, because elements will change as you refine your idea and move toward implementing it.
howToDoIt: Print a Business Model Canvas for each team member, or use an online version.
Fill in the sections together as a team. Expect holes the first time. It is acceptable not to know exactly how everything will work.
Pause to research when you need more information, then return to the sheet.
Reflect on the completed canvas to find gaps, ask questions, and compare costs with revenue streams.
Post the canvas in your workspace and revisit it. Make a new one as your project progresses.
whatYouNeed: A Business Model Canvas worksheet, printed or digital
tips: Find the gaps in the business model, ask questions, and be innovative.
Plan your strategy from the completed canvas.
Complete a new canvas as the idea changes, because the model will be refined along with the idea.
mistakes: Treating the canvas like a checklist.
Declaring it finished and not looking at the model again.
Being unclear about the timing of your plans.
Leaving out the numbers, so qualitative and quantitative data are not put together.
Packing in too much information.
methods.example:
An architecture firm is trying to figure out how to sell its designs to clients. Sales are going down even though the designs are spectacular. The firm completes a Business Model Canvas and finds gaps in its model.

IDEO.org and Water and Sanitation for the Urban Poor (WSUP) used a canvas to shape a business model for a pit latrine emptying service in Zambia. The canvas mapped partners, activities, and the value offered to customers, and it gave the team a quick check of costs against revenue streams to see whether the service could be sustainable (IDEO.org, 2015).

methods.name: Business Origami
methods.imageAlt: Business Origami model of a ride-hailing service, built from paper figures and sticky notes on a whiteboard, with arrows showing flows between rider, driver, and company.
methods.imageSource: Service Design Network, Business Origami, Touchpoint (Medium), 2019
methods.whatItIs: Business origami lets project stakeholders simulate how a system works through paper prototypes. Paper-cutout tokens stand for the actors, artifacts, environments, and technologies in the system, and arrows labeled with the value exchanged show how they interact (Martin & Hanington, 2012). The method also helps designers view the system from a user's perspective.
whenToUse: When you need to understand the reasoning behind the success of a model or system.
When you are researching how users move through or interact in a space.
For identifying the value of human interactions, relationships, and exchanges in a system.
howToDoIt: Identify the focus.
Prepare the resources, such as paper cutouts, sticky notes, and markers.
Place the items on a flat surface.
Explain the goal of the system.
Build the model. Draw arrows between the pieces and label each arrow with the value that is exchanged.
Identify pain points or challenges in the system.
Move pieces around to experiment with different layouts.
tips: Categorize the elements of the prototype to prevent confusion. For example, color code the main characters or users so they remain the focus of the group.
Use the model as a stage on which a scenario plays out over time, so the group can tell a story with it.
mistakes: Moving off target by focusing too much on individual pieces, such as the characters. The goal is to simulate how the system operates as a whole, based on how its elements interact.
methods.example: Business Origami can be used to simulate a hospital system. For example, paper cutouts can be used to represent patients, staff, or rooms. By physically replicating the workflow, designers can predict or document the behaviors of various people in the system.
sources: Martin, B., & Hanington, B. (2012). Universal methods of design. Rockport Publishers.
Chenghan Ke. (2018, August 15). Business origami: A method for service design. Medium. https://medium.com/@hankkechenghan/business-origami-valuable-method-for-service-design-43a882880627

methods.name: Cognitive Walkthrough
methods.imageAlt: Infographic titled How to Conduct a Cognitive Walkthrough with five numbered steps: define user profiles and goals, select tasks, create task descriptions, walk through each task, and document issues.
methods.imageSource: a graphic published by Trymata, whose logo appears in the image
methods.whatItIs: A cognitive walkthrough is an expert usability inspection method in which designers step through a task as if they were a new user. It evaluates whether the order of cues and prompts in a system matches how people cognitively process tasks and anticipate the next step, so the team can find the points where users might get confused or stuck. The method was introduced in the early 1990s by Polson, Lewis, Rieman, and Wharton (Martin & Hanington, 2012).
whenToUse: When you are testing early designs or prototypes, especially to examine the first-time user experience.
When you want to identify usability issues before testing with real users.
When you are evaluating how intuitive a process is.
When the system is meant for walk-up-and-use situations with no training or coaching, such as ATMs, parking meters, ticketing machines, and automated voice-response phone systems.
When users will not be available to test every step of the iterative design process.
howToDoIt: Choose representative tasks: Select a series of tasks a user would complete, written from the user's point of view.
Break each task into steps: Outline a believable sequence of actions the user would take.
Walk through each step as a new user: Step through the sequence as if you had never seen the system.

Ask four questions at every step: Will users want to produce the effect this action has? Will users see the control (button, menu, label) for the action? Once they find the control, will they recognize that it will produce the effect they want? After the action is taken, will they understand the feedback so they can confidently continue to the next action?
Record problems: Note any confusion or unclear elements, and use those observations to suggest improvements.
Revise and review again: Fix the weak steps, and decide which sequence creates the fewest obstacles for the user.
whatYouNeed: A clear task scenario with its action steps
A way to record notes, such as a form listing the four questions
Two or more reviewers, for different perspectives
tips: Do not assume prior knowledge when stepping through the task.
Focus on clarity rather than speed, and make sure each step is clearly understandable.
Use the walkthrough together with usability testing. The two methods tend to uncover different classes of problems.
mistakes: Skipping small steps, which are often where confusion happens.
Assuming users already know the system or have been trained to use it.
Using the walkthrough in place of usability testing instead of alongside it.
methods.example:
A team designing a mobile app uses a cognitive walkthrough to test how a new user signs up. As they go through the steps, they realize the sign-up button is not clearly labeled or easy to find. They adjust the design to make the process more intuitive.

In a classic example, evaluators walk through the task "Pay for two hours of parking with a credit card" at a parking meter. At the first action, selecting the two-hour option, they ask the four questions and note where a first-time user would be unsure what to do next (Martin & Hanington, 2012).

Wharton, C., Rieman, J., Lewis, C., & Polson, P. (1994). The cognitive walkthrough method: A practitioner's guide. In J. Nielsen & R. L. Mack (Eds.), Usability inspection methods (pp. 105-140). John Wiley & Sons.

methods.name: Desirability Testing
methods.imageAlt: Venn diagram of three overlapping circles labeled desirability, viability, and feasibility.
methods.imageSource: Ideation, Media Innovation and Entrepreneurship, as stated by the student
methods.whatItIs: Desirability testing gives users a list of positive, neutral, and negative adjectives to describe how a prototype makes them feel. After users select the cards that match their feelings, the researcher asks them to explain their choices.
whenToUse: When you are in the prototyping phase and want to identify which features of a prototype range from attractive to unpleasant.
When you need to learn which features would work in a design and how appealing they would be to users.
When you want to judge the effectiveness of features in an app or interface, based on their placement or appearance.
When you want to know whether a household appliance includes features users would be content to use every day.
When you are refining software for a final product and need to know what to change.
howToDoIt: Create: Build a prototype or mockup based on your team's current research problem, goal, or product.
Write the adjectives: On notecards or in an online tool, write a list of positive, neutral, and negative adjectives that could describe your prototype.
Gather users: Recruit people who match the audience for your product or service.
Explain: Describe the instructions and goal of the activity to participants.
Start the session: Ask each user to pick three to five adjectives that match the feelings they associate with the prototype and its features.
Learn: Ask users to explain why they chose each word, so you can apply the answers to improve future prototypes.
Repeat: Run the process with multiple users and with each new prototype, until the prototype draws only positive adjectives or the reaction you want.
whatYouNeed: Notecards, sticky notes, or paper cut into individual pieces, or an online tool that lets you type and move text around
tips: Give users space to judge the prototype freely, without interference or bias.
Explain what the product or service does, so users can judge it with that information.
When users explain their word choices, also note their body language and any activity that shows how they feel about the product.
mistakes: Using too many words of one kind. Include enough positive, neutral, and negative terms for users to describe their feelings fully.
Using terms that are vague or irrelevant to the prototype.
methods.example: A team of designers for a gaming chair would like to know how their current prototype makes users feel. Since their product is directed primarily towards gamers or individuals who desire comfort while sitting at their desk for long periods of time, they would ask a group of these individuals to evaluate their prototype. With the adjectives on the notecards, users are able to describe whether or not the product elicits a positive, neutral, or negative feeling based on the current design. Designers can then ask why the current design makes them feel the way it does, and if the reaction is not what designers are aiming for, they can continue creating different prototypes based on the adjectives until they get the desired reaction.
sources: User Interviews. (n.d.). Preference testing: Desirability studies for UX research. https://www.userinterviews.com/ux-research-field-guide-chapter/preference-testing
Hanington, B., & Martin, B. (2012). Universal methods of design. Rockport Publishers.
Barnum, C. (2022, November 3). Microsoft's product reaction cards: User satisfaction. UX Firm. https://www.uxfirm.com/microsofts-product-reaction-cards-unlock-user-satisfaction

methods.name: Experience Prototyping
methods.imageAlt: Man at a kitchen counter touching a large touchscreen built into the cabinet, which displays several graphs, next to a microwave.
methods.imageSource: Martin and Hanington (2012), Universal Methods of Design
methods.whatItIs: Experience prototyping surrounds a prototype with a simulated physical or social context so people can engage with it actively and subjectively. Whereas many prototypes only invite passive viewing, an experience prototype lets designers, clients, and users encounter a live experience of a product, system, service, or space.
whenToUse: When you need to better understand an existing users experiences and context.
When communicating ideas to an audience and or a group of individuals.
When furthering evaluating and exploring design ideas.
howToDoIt: Prepare the prototype: Build the prototype so people can experience it. Do not worry about appearance or cost, because the prototype is meant to be rough around the edges. It should allow active participation, which is key to the method.

Determine your desired results: Decide whether you are testing the experience to gain critical insight or using it as a communication tool to persuade key audiences. Ask what you are trying to gain from the experience.

Plan the scenario: Determine the location, who is involved, and any other details that will contribute to your desired results. If the goal is communication, for example, choose a location that can accommodate an audience. Make sure the user or client is recruited appropriately.
Execute the scenario: Foster a sense of the user's potential experience. Let the user work with the prototype with little to no guidance or interference, unless guidance is what you want to test.
Review your findings: Ask what you learned through active participation and whether everything went smoothly. If improvement is needed, note the issues and how they could be resolved.
whatYouNeed: Prototype of a product, system service, or space to interact with
tips: Take advantage of the low cost of this method. Low-fidelity props and role-playing are enough for early exploration.
When using the prototype to persuade an audience, make clear that it represents work in progress and not the final design.
mistakes: Focusing more on the formality of the toolkit rather than developing skills to better solve design problems.
Neglecting that different activities may require a different environment and or resources.
Planning too intricate of a prototype to where the usability becomes lost in translation.
methods.example: A doctor's office desires a new app to help their patients schedule appointments on their own rather than having to call. However, before they release this product they would like to test it out. A researcher plays the role of an elderly patient at home attempting to navigate the app in order to foster a vivid sense of how the target user may be feeling. The researcher provides critical feedback based on their interactions with the prototype, suggesting room for improvement via a more digestible interface.
sources: Buchenau, M., & Suri, J. F. (2000). Experience prototyping. Proceedings of the Conference on Designing Interactive Systems: Processes, Practices, Methods, and Techniques (DIS '00). https://doi.org/10.1145/347642.347802
Davidoff, S. (2010). Routine as a resource for the design of learning systems. https://doi.org/10.1145/1864431.1864486
Hanington, B., & Martin, B. (2012). Universal methods of design. Rockport Publishers.

methods.name: Heuristic Evaluation
methods.imageAlt: Poster set of the ten usability heuristics on a wall above an armchair.
methods.whatItIs: Heuristic evaluation is a usability engineering method in which one or more experts compare an interface design against a list of rules of thumb, called heuristics. Unlike user testing, where you watch real users try to use the product, a few experts walk through the design to find common usability problems. It catches bugs and confusing parts of a layout before you spend money building something that does not work.
whenToUse: When you have a wireframe, prototype, or finished product and want to find obvious "low-hanging fruit" bugs.
When you don't have the budget or time to recruit a dozen users for a full study.
Early in the design process to ensure the "basics" of good design are being followed.
howToDoIt: Select your Heuristics: Most people use Jakob Nielsen's "10 Usability Heuristics".
Define the Scenarios: Pick a few specific tasks (like "Check out a guest" or "Change my profile picture").
Walk Through the Interface: Go through the tasks step-by-step and note every time a rule is broken.
Assign Severity: For every issue you find, rate it on a scale (0 = not a problem, 5 = usability catastrophe).
Compile the Report: Document the problem, which heuristic it violated, and a suggestion on how to fix it.
whatYouNeed: A list of heuristics, such as Nielsen's ten usability heuristics (for example, consistency and standards, error prevention, flexibility and efficiency of use, aesthetic and minimalist design, and help and documentation)
tips: Be specific. Do not just say "this page is confusing." Say something like, "this violates 'Consistency and Standards' because the 'Submit' button is red here but green on the last page."
Note what is working well, so the designers do not change those parts by accident.
Have each expert evaluate alone first, then meet to compare notes so evaluators do not influence each other's opinions.
mistakes: Evaluating as "just a user." Experts should look for violations of the heuristics, not personal opinions such as "I don't like this shade of blue."
Using only one evaluator. One person's bias can miss major issues, so multiple perspectives are key.
Giving vague explanations. If you do not name the specific heuristic that was broken, the design team will not know how to fix the problem systematically.
methods.example: Imagine a freshman is using a new campus app to book a treadmill at the gym. While doing a Heuristic Evaluation, the evaluator notices that after hitting "Confirm," there is no "Success" message…the app just jumps back to the home screen. This violates the "Visibility of System Status" heuristic because the student is not sure if their reservation actually went through or if the app crashed. To fix this, the evaluator suggests adding a confirmation pop-up or a green checkmark so the student knows exactly what happened.

methods.name: Live Prototyping

library.book: The Field Guide to Human-Centered Design (IDEO.org, 2015)
library.title: Live Prototyping

methods.whatItIs: Live prototyping is an experiential testing method that evaluates concepts within real-world environments to observe authentic user behaviors and collect feedback. It generates practical insights about how a solution functions in context, identifying specific areas that require further iteration and refinement.
whenToUse: When testing how a concept performs in a real-life environment.
When exploring service design, customer interactions, or user journeys.
When you need to compare multiple variations of a solution in real time.
When you need behavioral data instead of making assumptions.
howToDoIt: Set a goal: Decide what you need to observe in the experiment.
Define the scope: Decide how long the live prototype needs to run and where it must take place.
Plan data collection: Identify the key indicators and the data collection tools that fit the logistics of your prototype.
Run variations: If you have the capacity, run a few prototypes at once to test variations of a solution quickly.
Keep critiquing: Review and adjust the design over multiple days.
Iterate: Try new approaches until your solution gets closer to the real thing.
tips: Keep prototypes simple and flexible so they can be adjusted quickly.
Focus on observing user behavior rather than asking leading questions.
Test in the actual context where the solution will be used.
Capture both qualitative and quantitative data.
Debrief immediately after testing to document insights.
mistakes: Making the prototype too complex.
Testing in an artificial environment instead of a real context.
Failing to define clear goals before the test begins.
Not revising the design based on the feedback you receive.
Ignoring unexpected user behaviors or edge cases.
methods.example: A healthcare team is testing a new patient check-in system and sets up a temporary version in a clinic waiting room. Patients interact with the system as they arrive, while staff take notes on how smoothly the process works. Based on real-time feedback and observed challenges, the team adjusts the design and tests improved versions over several days.
sources: IDEO.org. (2015). The field guide to human-centered design. IDEO.org. https://www.designkit.org/methods/live-prototyping
Liedtka, J., & Ogilvie, T. (2011). Designing for growth: A design thinking toolkit for managers. Columbia University Press.
Martin, R. (2009). The design of business: Why design thinking is the next competitive advantage. Harvard Business Press.

methods.name: Parallel Prototyping
methods.imageAlt: Diagram comparing parallel prototyping, where two prototypes lead to one final prototype at the same time, with iterative prototyping, where one prototype leads to the next.
methods.whatItIs: Simultaneously creating and testing multiple distinct design directions before finalizing a single solution.
whenToUse: When you want to keep design teams from focusing on one design too early in the process.
When teams are looking for better, more effective design results.
When you want to prototype but are not yet set on a solution.
When the project timeframe is short, because prototype ideas can be created quickly.
howToDoIt: Research, gain insight, and ideate: Complete the earlier steps of the design process first, so the prototypes rest on enough background to be effective.
Review your solutions: Look back at the solutions the team has thought up and consider how they could be implemented together in designs.

Prototype multiple designs: The most important part of the method is prototyping several ideas at once. Keep the prototypes simple, for example on paper for ease of use or in other materials, as long as they still convey the meaning of each design. The prototypes will evolve through the process.
Discuss and review: As designers, review the prototypes together, look for connections, and discuss what worked well and what worked poorly in each.
Connect: Use what each prototype did well to inform the final product.
whatYouNeed: Materials for prototyping (Tape, Scissors, Colored pencils, etc.)
tips: Paper prototyping is perfect to implement into this process. Paper is inexpensive and easily malleable to fit the needs of a designer creating prototypes.
Encourage collaboration and discussion amongst the group creating the prototypes. The more people working together and bouncing ideas off of each other, the better.
mistakes: Don't be married to an idea. Just because you come up with a great idea and prototype it, doesn't mean you shouldn't explore other options.

Don't just come up with a few designs. The point here is to test as many ideas as possible, so it is essential that multiple prototypes are created. The more ideas tested, the better the final product will be.
methods.example: A design firm is working on a design for a new case for a folding phone. Because the phone design is intricate, the case needs to be created to fit the standards of the phone. They have a bunch of ideas that need testing, so they go with Parallel Prototyping to envision as many of their ideas as possible. Through this method, they are able to make multiple designs to account for the hinge in the phone, and figure out how they will design their folding phone case.
sources: Martin, B., & Hanington, B. (2012). Universal methods of design: 100 ways to research complex problems, develop innovative ideas, and design effective solutions. Rockport Publishers.
Hohl, M. (2017). Prototyping: Iterative vs. Parallel. Medium. https://medium.com/ucsddesignco/iterative-vs-parallel-prototyping-575d455da5b5
Kesari, S. (2019, September 24). Parallel Prototyping. IXDPratt. https://ixd.prattsi.org/2019/09/parallel-prototyping/

methods.name: Rapid Iterative Testing & Evaluation
methods.imageAlt: Diagram of the RITE process that repeats the cycle of run participant and make changes three times, captioned Figure 13.1, RITE testing versus standard usability testing.
methods.whatItIs: Rapid Iterative Testing and Evaluation (RITE) is a formative usability method that fixes issues as they arise instead of saving them for a large session at the end. The team tests with one participant, changes the prototype as soon as a problem is identified and the team agrees on a solution, and then retests the fix with more participants (Martin & Hanington, 2012).
whenToUse: When you need to understand how to improve a current system.
When you are trying to identify problems you may not see.
When you are dealing with a small sample size.
When you need results quickly.
howToDoIt: Define: Define the task you are testing and declare your goals.
Ideate: Brainstorm ideas that could work as a solution.
Establish Group: Find participants; this can be a small group.
Selection: Test one of these ideas (it does not have to be perfect, just have a testable process).
Test: Have one person go through the process, take notes on where they struggle.
Solve: Fix these issues immediately.
Repeat: Repeat the testing process with different people until a few users pass with no issues.
whatYouNeed: Notebook or a way to take notes of findings
tips: Fix issues as they come, and don't focus on making the fix perfect on the first try.
Test users in small groups.
Don't fix things that seem to be preference over function; take note of preferences and fix them if they become a pattern.
Focus on big issues first and then move to preferences.
Don't give specific instructions; it defeats the purpose of having the user try to figure it out.
mistakes: Telling the participant exactly what to do.
Allowing many people to use the system before making changes.
Fixing EVERY issue, sometimes things are a preference, fix the issues that cause major issues.
methods.example: A local coffee shop has a hard time keeping up with the orders as well as taking orders. To fix this, they want to implement multiple kiosks in the shop to improve efficiency. They develop a paper prototype that simulates their current system and have 10 customers use it, one at a time. After each customer uses the system, they take notes on areas of struggle and fix them right away before the next person uses the system, until no more issues are found.
sources: Drachen, A., Mirza-Babaei, P., & Nacke, L. E. (Eds.). (2018). Games user research. Oxford University Press.
Medlock, M. C., Wixon, D., McGee, M., & Welsh, D. (n.d.). Chapter 17: The rapid iterative test and evaluation method: Better products in less time.
Wigdor, D., & Wixon, D. (2011). Brave NUI world: Designing natural user interfaces for touch and gesture. Morgan Kaufmann.

methods.name: Role-Playing
methods.imageAlt: One student sits in an office chair fitted with a cardboard car prop while another leans over to push it.

library.book: The Field Guide to Human-Centered Design (IDEO.org, 2015)
library.title: Role Playing

methods.whatItIs: Role-playing physically acts out a proposed service experience to identify areas of frustration. It provides insight when direct observation is not feasible or ethical.
whenToUse: When you need to analyze the consumer perspective.
When you need to figure out what is working and what is not.
In the early stages of prototyping, to address pain points early.
When you want to test a product or service.
howToDoIt: Research: Base the scenario on grounded research, such as interviews and observations.
Identify: Decide what you want to test in the scenario.

Assign roles: Give each team member a role, such as note taker, facilitator, or actor. Use separate team members as the actor and the note taker, because actors cannot document their performance while staying in character.
Document: Use videos, photos, and notes to record the session.
Enact: Imitate the real-world scenario as closely as possible. Improvisation is encouraged and makes sure the actor encounters some user error.
Debrief: After the session, hold a thorough discussion of your observations.
whatYouNeed: One person as the observer and note taker
tips: Do not stick to a set script. Analyze as many pain points as possible.
Make sure your research is based on real-world observations or documentation, and do not make assumptions.
mistakes: Having no think-aloud protocol.
Not properly addressing user error.
Running a straightforward role-playing experience that does not address any pain points.
methods.example: Your team is tasked with creating a new website for a retirement home, but the team is not allowed to talk directly to the residents. It relies on knowledge gathered online, builds a mockup of the website, and assigns roles: a note taker, a facilitator, and someone who portrays an elderly resident who needs to navigate the site. After the role-play, the team enlarges the font so the text is more readable and simplifies the website to make it easier to navigate.
sources: Hanington, B., & Martin, B. (2012). Universal methods of design. Rockport Publishers.
IDEO.org. (2015). The field guide to human-centered design. https://www.designkit.org/resources/1.html
Rodgers, P. A., & Yee, J. (2023). The Routledge companion to design research. Routledge. https://doi.org/10.4324/9781003182443

methods.name: Scenario Description Swimlanes
methods.imageAlt: Blank scenario description template with a row of seven storyboard frames above swimlanes labeled actions, actors involved, touchpoints, and business process lane.
methods.whatItIs: Scenario description swimlanes are a way to visually map different elements, whether that be teams or individuals, as they follow the sequence of a process.
whenToUse: When you want to map the user experience and flow throughout a user's encounter with the design being researched.
When you are early in the design process, because it gives you time to work out the issues you find and to interview each party at the steps presented.
When you need to compare multiple lanes that represent different actors, which makes the method useful for complex systems with multiple teams.
When you need to break complicated macro experiences into micro interactions between many moving parts.
howToDoIt: Define the scenario: Become familiar with the situation the swimlanes will represent, and decide whether it is a user flow, a system interaction, or an organizational workflow.

Identify the lanes: The core lanes are a storyboard lane (graphics or a comic that visualizes each step), a user experience lane (flowcharts that give insight into the corresponding storyboard steps), a business lane (business logic and further context for stakeholders), and a tools and systems lane (the technology behind the design and how it should interact at each phase). Add other lanes as the project requires.
Validate the swimlanes: Talk with stakeholders and users through interviews or further prototype testing to validate or critique the diagram.
Refine the diagram: Use what you learned during validation to edit and improve the swimlanes for accuracy.
whatYouNeed: A well-rounded understanding of the linear process the swimlanes will replicate
Physical or digital tools to create the diagram (digital is recommended because it is easier to edit)
Model users to interview on the accuracy of the swimlanes
tips: Stick to simple descriptions and precise drawings to keep the goal clear.
Color-code the lane to create visual continuity and distinction.
Lucidchart and Miro are digital tools recommended for use in visual mapping projects like this.
mistakes: Using too many lanes, because the goal of scenario description swimlanes is to simplify complex systems.
Not labeling connectors or explaining how to get from one stage to the next.
Not focusing on a specific user story, which produces a confusing swimlane that lacks direction.
methods.example: Scenario description swimlanes would be useful for an online shopping experience with multiple channels. The method can map how in-store reservations, shipping details, and email confirmations work together to create the user's experience of the complex system.
sources: Conole, G. (2013). Designing for learning in an open world. Springer.

Martin, B., & Hanington, B. (2012). Universal methods of design: 100 ways to research complex problems, develop innovative ideas, and design effective solutions. Choice Reviews Online, 49(10). https://doi.org/10.5860/choice.49-5403

Pouya, S. (2024, November 19). Swimlane diagram: A UX designer's secret weapon for order in chaos. Medium. https://sepantapouya.medium.com/swimlane-diagram-a-ux-designers-secret-weapon-for-order-in-chaos-fb9aa00927d5

methods.name: Stakeholder Walkthrough
methods.imageAlt: A woman presents at a whiteboard with sticky notes to colleagues seated around a table in an office.
methods.whatItIs: Inviting co-designers or others stakeholders into the research synthesis process is an effective way to accurately surface key themes and to identify the most critical and novel insights and opportunities. Bringing community co-designers into the synthesis process helps to raise the voice and expertise of those closest to the problem.
whenToUse: After gathering research data, when the team needs to make sense of what they learned and identify shared themes.
After interviews, observations, or field research, once data collection is complete and the team needs to organize notes, patterns, and key takeaways.
When you are working on complex or community-based problems, where different perspectives matter and meaning should not be defined only by the design team.
When you are identifying priorities and opportunities for ideation, before concept generation, so the design direction is grounded in shared understanding.
howToDoIt: Gather research notes and observations: Bring together notes, quotes, interview takeaways, and any other collected data.
Hold a download session: Ask everyone involved in the research to share what stood out, surprises, repeated ideas, and important moments.
Create an initial rough synthesis: The design team groups notes into early themes or categories before meeting with the wider group.
Bring stakeholders or co-designers together: Present the draft themes and invite participants to react, discuss, and build on them.
Ask guiding questions: For example: Do these themes feel accurate? What is missing? What feels most important or surprising? Does the language reflect people's experiences?
Refine and prioritize themes: Adjust wording, combine ideas, and decide which themes matter most.
Develop insight statements: A smaller team turns the final themes into clear insight statements, then shares them back with the wider group for feedback.
tips: Come in with an early draft of themes so the session has structure.
Treat participants as experts, not just reviewers.
Use direct quotes from interviews to ground discussion in real experiences.
Keep themes short, clear, and easy to understand.
Focus on patterns and meaning rather than trying to include every single detail.
mistakes: Skipping the initial synthesis. Starting with raw data can make the session overwhelming.
Letting the design team dominate interpretation. This can reduce the value of stakeholder perspectives.
Using vague or academic language. Themes should reflect how participants actually talk about their experiences.
Focusing only on agreement. Tension, disagreement, and surprises can point to deeper insights.
methods.example: A design team interviews people about their experience using a public service. After the interviews, the team groups notes into early themes such as confusion, waiting time, and unclear instructions. They then meet with participants to review the themes and ask what feels accurate, what is missing, and what stands out most. Together, they refine the themes and use them to identify key insights for the next phase of the project.
sources: Flowers, E., & Miller, M. (2023). Your guide to blueprinting the practical way (2nd ed.). Practical by Design. https://www.practicalbydesign.co
IDEO.org. (2015). The field guide to human-centered design (1st ed.). IDEO.org. https://www.designkit.org/resources/1
Martin, B., & Hanington, B. (2012). Universal methods of design: 100 ways to research complex problems, develop innovative ideas, and design effective solutions. Rockport Publishers.
methods.editorNote: As defined in Universal Methods of Design (Martin & Hanington, 2012, p. 168), a stakeholder walkthrough is a group usability inspection in which end users, stakeholders, and the design team step through a task-based scenario together from the end user's perspective. This card describes a related participatory practice: co-synthesizing research findings with stakeholders and community co-designers.

methods.name: Storyboarding
methods.imageAlt: Three columns of pencil storyboard frames showing a sequence of action scenes.

library.book: The Field Guide to Human-Centered Design (IDEO.org, 2015)
library.title: Storyboard

methods.whatItIs: Storyboarding is a visual prototyping method that illustrates a user's experience over time through a sequence of shots. It helps teams explore, communicate, and test how a product or service will be used in a more realistic context.
whenToUse: When you want to visualize a user journey from start to finish.
When testing ideas before investing in a more detailed product.
When you need to communicate concepts to stakeholders or teammates.
When identifying gaps, pain points, or missed opportunities in an experience.
When you are exploring how multiple touchpoints connect over time.
howToDoIt: Define the scenario: Choose a specific persona, goal, and situation to focus the storyboard on. Be clear about what experience you are illustrating exactly.
Identify key moments: Break the experience into major steps or interactions that the user goes through over time.
Sketch each frame: Draw simple visuals for each step in sequence, and focus on clarity rather than artistic quality.
Add context and captions: Include short descriptions of user actions and environmental details to explain what is happening in each frame.
Include user perspective: Show what the user is thinking and feeling in reaction to the actions in the experience.
Review the flow: Check that the sequence makes sense logically and represents a realistic scenario.
Refine and iterate: Revise the storyboard based on feedback and use it to guide prototype development.
tips: Keep drawings simple and easy to understand.
Focus on the user's experience, not just the interface.
Show emotions and context to make story more realistic.
Use storyboards early to explore ideas quickly.
Iterate based on feedback and newly gained insights.
mistakes: Adding too much detail and slowing the process.
Skipping important steps in the user journey.
Making unrealistic scenarios.
Ignoring user emotion or context.
Treating the storyboard as final instead of iterative.
methods.example: A team designing a campus navigation app creates a storyboard to show a student trying to find a classroom in an unfamiliar building. The frames depict searching for directions, following a step-by-step guide, and arriving at the destination. Through this process, the team finds the source of confusion from indoor navigation and adds clearer visual cues and real-time updates to improve the experience before creating a prototype.
sources: Hanington, B., & Martin, B. (2019). Universal methods of design, expanded and revised. Rockport Publishers.
van der Lelie, C. (2005, September 22). The value of storyboards in the product design process. Personal and Ubiquitous Computing. https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/S00779-005-0026-7
Storyboarding. (n.d.). Proceedings of the 6th Conference on Designing Interactive Systems. ACM. https://dl.acm.org/doi/10.1145/1142405.1142410

methods.name: Think-Aloud Protocol
methods.imageAlt: Mobile app screen titled 5 steps to list, with fields to add a photo, write a title, and write a description, captured from a recorded think-aloud session.
methods.imageNote: Cropped to remove the participant from view.
methods.whatItIs: Thinking-Aloud Protocol is a research method in which users say their thoughts out loud while they are performing the task. This helps researchers understand how users make decisions and fix the problem. It creates verbal data (what people say) that later can be analysed to understand real thoughts, feelings, and reasoning to fix a problem.
whenToUse: When you are testing new interfaces, prototypes, or websites, to pinpoint where users get stuck or are unclear about the task and to see why challenges happen.
When you are running one-on-one activities that require navigation tasks or organizing information through specific actions.
When researchers need fast feedback to improve a product, so they understand what to fix and why before the final product.
howToDoIt: Find the goal or problem that is to be investigated. E.g. decision making.
Create practical tasks that users can finish during a session.
Write out instructions and specify that users should voice out everything they are thinking while performing the task.
Watch the users while they are completing the task and voice their thoughts, and record the actions and comments.
Go through the recorded notes, audios or videos taken and find patterns, themes and issues presented in the users behaviors or thoughts.
whatYouNeed: Consent forms to record and photograph
Computer, camera, microphone, or phone (if allowed)
2 researchers to go through the task and document it
tips: Reassure the user that the one being tested is the product, not them.
Softly let the users know to keep voicing their thoughts if the go silent.
Remember not to influence the users actions, let them act and think naturally.
Record the session (notes/audio/video) to analyze later.
When analysing the data, make groups of common patterns and repeated issues.
mistakes: Asking questions like "was it confusing?" which lead to biased answers.
Interrupting the user while they complete the task, which hides their full, natural behavior.
Letting silence run on, because users may forget to verbalize their thoughts.
Talking too much, which can overload the user and affect their performance.
Taking every comment too literally instead of looking for patterns in behavior and thoughts.
methods.example: An entrepreneur father has created a meal planning and shopping list app where families can create groups and see their dinner plans recipes, generate menus or add items to the grocery list, in addition to circles to find new recipes and share ideas with others. The owner of the app wants to know what difficulties can a user find when navigating through the app on their first time using it. He decides to ask his family members to try the app while narrating their experience using it, from the moment they download it to the moment they have used four different features: "menu, recipe, circle and family, pantry". While navigating the app the family members voiced comments like "If I share a recipe in spanish would it translate it into the other family members language?" "If I join with the family code, do my other family members in my circle need to use the code too?" "can I only be in one family?" "can I share youtube recipes to the app". "This button is weird, why does it look like that" followed by "Oh, it's a plate with a measuring spoon" This helped the creator understand that there were some limitations to his app, and the family feature could use some improvement. The combination of verbal feedback and behavior observations allowed the creator to find some faults in his product.
sources: Baxter, K., Courage, C., & Caine, K. (2015). Think aloud protocol. ScienceDirect Topics. https://www.sciencedirect.com/topics/computer-science/think-aloud-protocol
Braithwaite, L. (n.d.). Think aloud protocol. The Decision Lab. https://thedecisionlab.com/reference-guide/design/think-aloud-protocol
O'Brien, L., & Wilson, S. (2023, May 26). Talking about thinking aloud: Perspectives from interactive think-aloud practitioners. Journal of User Experience (JUX).

methods.name: Usability Report
methods.imageAlt: AI-generated sample usability report for a food ordering app, with key metrics, a chart of issues by severity, and a table of detailed findings.
methods.whatItIs: A usability report is a structured document that summarizes findings from usability testing. It identifies user issues, patterns, and insights, and provides recommendations to improve a design.
whenToUse: When evaluating a prototype or product.
After conducting usability testing sessions.
When communicating findings to stakeholders.
When prioritizing design improvements.
Before finalizing or launching a design.
howToDoIt: Conduct usability testing: Observe users interacting with a product or prototype.
Record observations: Take notes on user behavior, errors, and feedback.
Identify key issues: Highlight recurring usability problems.
Organize findings: Group issues into categories such as navigation, usability, or content.
Prioritize problems: Rank issues based on severity and impact.
Develop recommendations: Suggest clear improvements for each issue.
Compile the report: Present findings in a structured and easy-to-read format.
tips: Focus on user behavior rather than assumptions.
Keep findings clear and concise.
Prioritize the most critical issues.
Use simple, non-technical language.
Support findings with evidence.
mistakes: Including too much unnecessary detail.
Ignoring patterns across multiple users.
Failing to prioritize issues.
Using vague recommendations.
Focusing on opinions instead of observed behavior.
methods.example: A design team tests a food delivery app with several users. During testing, they observe that multiple users struggle to locate the checkout button. In the usability report, this issue is categorized as high priority, and the team recommends redesigning the button placement and improving its visibility. This helps improve the overall user experience before launch.
sources: Nielsen, J. (1993). Usability engineering. Nielsen Norman Group. https://www.nngroup.com/books/usability-engineering/
Rubin, J., & Chisnell, D. (2008). Handbook of usability testing: How to plan, design, and conduct effective tests (2nd ed.). Wiley.
Nielsen Norman Group. (n.d.). Usability testing 101. https://www.nngroup.com/articles/usability-testing-101/
Interaction Design Foundation. (2016, June 2). What is usability testing? https://ixdf.org/literature/topics/usability-testing

methods.name: Usability Testing
methods.imageAlt: Illustration of a researcher in a lab coat observing a participant who works on a laptop at a desk.
methods.whatItIs: Observing real users as they perform a series of tasks to see how they interact with an interface or product.
whenToUse: Before launching a product to the public, to uncover major bugs or mistakes.
After big changes to the product that could affect usability.
Before pilot testing with a wider audience.
When you are focusing on task-based or goal-based testing.
howToDoIt: Define your tasks: Come up with five to eight tasks for your user to complete.
Find participants: Recruit people within your target audience.
Develop a script: Write a script your moderator will use to introduce the tasks and debrief the task and the product.
Conduct the test: Have participants speak their process out loud, and screen record the test. Remain a neutral party while running it.
Analyze your findings: Identify pain points, confusion, or issues.
Improve: Use the findings to improve your product.
whatYouNeed: A device to conduct the test on, such as a mobile phone or laptop
tips: Use a think-aloud method paired with detailed note taking to identify pain points.
Record the screen and audio so you can look back on the session.
Hold a pre-test and post-test interview to gauge feelings.
mistakes: Testing with the wrong audience.
Lacking in sample size.
Asking leading questions that place bias in the mind of the tester.
Unclear tasks for the user to complete can lead to frustration and abandonment of the task all together.
Neglecting alternate device interfaces. If the product works for phone and computer both should be tested.
methods.example: Bookshop.org wants to improve its website and has made major changes in hopes of improvement. It recruits a test group of five to eight people who frequently buy books online and writes five basic tasks that test the new features. The team finds that most people pause and struggle with the new filter options, and it improves that function afterward.

methods.name: Wizard of Oz
methods.imageAlt: Woman seated at a desk using a laptop while a large wall screen shows an app prototype and a small video call window.
methods.whatItIs: A method where a human (the "Wizard") simulates the backend functionality of a system from behind the scenes while the user interacts with what they believe is a fully autonomous interface.
whenToUse: When the technology required (Like voice recognition or AI technology) is too expensive or complex to build for a test.
When you need to test user reactions to a system's logic before writing any code.
When exploring interaction patterns for new technological ideas.
When you want to validate if a specific automated service actually provides value to users.
howToDoIt: Identify the specific automated functions that need to be simulated.
Set up the interface that the user will interact with.
Establish a communication channel (like a hidden script or remote screen) for the "Wizard" to receive what the user is doing.
Define the "Wizard's" rules and response time to ensure consistency.
Conduct the test with a participant while the "Wizard" manually triggers the system's responses from another room or hidden desk.
Debrief the participant to understand their experience and reveal the simulation if necessary for the research.
whatYouNeed: Low or medium fidelity interface (like a screen or physical box)
Communication tools (like a remote desktop or physical wires)
tips: The "Wizard" must be fast and consistent. Any lag or human-like behavior can break the illusion and skew the results.
mistakes: Revealing the simulation to the user before the test ends, which breaks the illusion.
Failing to define a clear script for the "Wizard," which leads to inconsistent interactions between participants.
methods.example: A startup is developing and testing their product of a voice-controlled mirror, in which they want to see if users would find if having a "outfit recommendations" feature would be helpful. Instead of building the complex technical AI system, a researcher sat in the next room acting as the "Wizard", listened to the user's requests through a microphone, and manually pushed pre-designed images of clothes to the mirror's screen.
